Section  205,  read with sections  199,  200  and  201, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deduction of tax at source  -  Bar against direct demand on assessee  (Scope of provision) - Assessment year  2024-25  - Assessee, employee, received salary after deduction of tax at source - However, employer company went into liquidation and did not deposit TDS deducted from salary in Government account - Assessee filed return claiming TDS credit - Assessing Officer raised a demand on account of denial of TDS credit due tomismatch with Form 26AS - Whether once tax was deducted by employer, assessee employee could not be forced to make good shortfall in deposit of tax by employer and revenue had to proceed against employer for recovery of said demand under section 200 and 201 - Held, yes - Whether thus, Assessing Officer was to be directed not to recover any demand from assessee - Held, yes [Paras 2.3 and 2.4] [In favour of assessee]

Section 205, read with section 199, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Illustrations) - Assessment years 2011-12 and 2012-13 - Assessee, a pilot by profession, was an employee of Kingfisher Airlines which had deducted tax at source from his salary but had not deposited amount to Central Government's account - Assessing Officer issued on assessee notice seeking recovery of outstanding demand - Whether in view of provisions of section 205 Assessing Officer shall not deny benefit of tax deducted at source by employer to assessee and shall give credit of TDS amount to him - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where employer deducted tax at source from assessee's salary but had not deposited amount with Central Govt. Assessing Officer would not deny benefit of tax deducted at source by employer to assessee

Section 205, read with section 199, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Illustrations) - Assessment years 2011-12 and 2012-13 - Assessee, a pilot by profession, was an employee of Kingfisher Airlines which had deducted tax at source from his salary but had not deposited amount to Central Government's account - Assessing Officer issued on assessee notice seeking recovery of outstanding demand - Whether in view of provisions of section 205 Assessing Officer shall not deny benefit of tax deducted at source by employer to assessee and shall give credit of TDS amount to him - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]   Circulars and Notifications : Office Memorandum F. No. 275/29/2014-IT(B), dated 11-3-2016

I. Section 205 of the Income-tax Act, 1961  - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Credit for TDS) - Whether where assessee had followed regime framed in Act for collecting tax at source albeit through an agent of Government, i.e., deductor, and since agent/deductor failed to deposit tax with Government, recovery proceedings could only be initiated against agent/deductor and not against assessee/deductee; credit for TDS amount could not be denied to assessee - Held, yes [Para 21.2 and 3] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where deductor failed to deposit tax with Government, recovery proceedings could only be initiated against agent/deductor and not against assessee/deductee; credit for TDS amount could not be denied to assessee  INCOME TAX : Section 199 could not come in way of granting credit of TDS to deductee

Section 199,  read with section 203, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted - Assessment year 1997-98 - Whether once an employer has deducted tax at source, employee-assessee cannot be held responsible for payment once again and any such demand raised against employee-assessee cannot be recovered - Held, yes - In respect of relevant assessment year, assessee claimed credit of tax deducted at source (TDS) by his employer from salary paid to him - Assessee submitted that tax had been deducted by employer every time salary was paid to him but employer had not furnished Form No. 16 or any other relevant evidence to prove that tax had been deducted from salary paid to him - In support of his claim, assessee could furnish copies of pay slips only for two months and in respect of remaining 10 months, he did not furnish any documentary evidence and submitted that he was not in a position to procure said details and certificate from his employer - Assessing Officer held that in absence of statutory certificate, credit for TDS could not be given to assessee - Whether it was duty of Assessing Officer to collect details of payment made by employer of assessee and if it was found that tax had been deducted from salary paid to assessee, no recovery could be made from him and if Assessing Officer was able to obtain TDS certificate itself, then credit had to be given to assessment account of assessee - Held, yes - Whether matter was to be remitted back to Assessing Officer for proceeding further to collect said details - Held, yes

I. Section 205 of the Income-tax Act, 1961  - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Credit for TDS) - Whether where assessee had followed regime framed in Act for collecting tax at source albeit through an agent of Government, i.e., deductor, and since agent/deductor failed to deposit tax with Government, recovery proceedings could only be initiated against agent/deductor and not against assessee/deductee; credit for TDS amount could not be denied to assessee - Held, yes [Para 21.2 and 3] [In favour of assessee]  II. Section 199 of the Income-tax Act, 1961  - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted (General) - Whether section 199 could not come in way of granting credit of TDS to deductee - Held, yes [Para 28] [In favour of assessee]

Section 205, read with section 199, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Illustration) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee's employer deducted tax at source while making payment of wages but not deposited to Government Account - Assessing Officer did not grant credit of TDS which had been deducted from wages of assessee - Whether matter was to be restored back to file of Assessing Officer to verify fact and grant set off of tax deducted as well as reflected in salary slip and pass order afresh - Held, yes [Para 4] [Matter remanded]INCOME TAX : Where assessee's employer deducted tax at source while making payment of wages but not deposited to Government Account and Assessing Officer did not grant credit of TDS to assessee, matter was to be restored back to Assessing Officer to verify fact and grant set off of tax deducted

Section  205,  read with section  199,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deduction of tax at source  -  Bar Against Direct Demand on Assessee  (Non-deposit of TDS) - Assessment year  2020-21 and 2021-22  - Assessee’s employer deducted tax at source from salary but failed to deposit same with Government - While processing return, Assessing Officer denied credit of such TDS to assessee due to system mismatch and raised demand - High Court held that in view of section 205 read with CBDT  Instruction No. 275 dated 1-6-2015  and Office Memorandum dated 11-3-2016, no demand could be raised against assessee where tax had been deducted but not deposited by the deductor - High Court further directed CBDT to modify software so that no demand could be raised in future in cases where there would be mismatch between TDS and tax not deposited by deductor in case of deductee - Whether since aforesaid directions had nothing to do with case on merits and would not affect assessee, direction issued for changes to be made in software were to be set aside - Held, yes [Para 5] [Partly in favour of revenue]

Section 205, read with section 199, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Illustration) - Assessment year 2016-17 - Assessee's employer deducted tax at source while making payment of wages but not deposited to Government Account - Assessing Officer did not grant credit of TDS which had been deducted from wages of assessee - Whether matter was to be restored back to file of Assessing Officer to verify fact and grant set off of tax deducted as well as reflected in salary slip and pass order afresh - Held, yes [Para 4] [Matter remanded]

Section 205, read with sections 234B and 234BC, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (TDS Credit) - Assessment year 2024-25 - Assessee, an employee, received gross salary from his employer - Employer deducted TDS from his salary but did not issue Form 16 - Assessee filed return declaring salary and claimed said TDS credit - While processing return under section 143(1), CPC denied TDS credit on ground that no corresponding TDS was available in Form 26AS and assessee failed to submit Form 16 and levied interest under sections 234B and 234C - It was noted that employer had not paid any TDS after deducting from employee and after deducting TDS neither remitted amount to Government account nor filed any quarterly returns - Further assessee was an ex-employee and, thus, was not in a position to acquire relevant document from company - Whether since assessee had brought on record relevant salary slips to demonstrate that tax was deducted from salary, revenue could not deny tax credit to assessee - Held, yes - Whether, accordingly, interest levied under sections 234B and 234C was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 7] [In favour of assessee].

Section 205 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Tax deducted at source) - Assessment years  2009-10  and 2011-12 - Assessee was employed with company KIL - During course of employment, KIL deducted TDS from assessee's salary but, KIL did not deposit same with Income-tax authorities - Accordingly, revenue raised demand against assessee - Assessee claimed that TDS was duly reflected in Form 16A issued by KIL and, thus, he was not liable to pay tax - Whether in view of decision in case of Sanjay Sudan v. Asstt. CIT [2023] 148 taxmann.com 329/292 Taxman 138/452 ITR 107 (Delhi), revenue could not recover TDS from assessee - Held, yes [Para 10] [In favour of assessee]

Section 205, read with  section 199, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Scope of provision) - Assessment years 2009-10, 2011-12 and 2012-13 - Employer paid salary to assessee after deduction of tax at source but did not deposit same with department - Assessing Officer did not allow credit of tax deducted at source and raised demand against assessee towards tax and interest - Whether assessee having accepted salary after deduction of tax at source had no further control over it and it was duty of employer to pay deducted tax to department and employer having failed to perform his duty to deposit deducted tax, assessee could not be penalized - Held, yes - Whether section 199 could not operate as impediment to grant relief to assessee and, thus, impugned demand deserved to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 8, 9 and 10] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where employer paid salary to assessee after deduction of tax at source but employer did not deposit same with department, assessee could not be penalized for failure of employer to perform his duty to deposit deducted tax

Section 199, read with sections 234B and 234C, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted (Illustrations) - Assessment years 2018-19 and 2019-20 - During year under consideration, assessee had earned salary income - It had claimed refund of TDS deducted under section 192 - Assessing Officer denied claim of TDS to assessee on ground that same was not reflecting in Form 26AS and consequently, had charged interest under sections 234B and 234C - Whether since assessee himself acting as MD and CEO of its company did not deduct TDS on salary paid/payable to himself for working as MD and CEO of company, he could not be allowed to take benefit of his own wrong and, thus, was not entitled to any claim of set-off of TDS, which was never deposited by company - Held, yes [Paras 12 and 13] [In favour of revenue]

Section 205 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar Against Direct Demand on Assessee (Non-deposit of TDS) - Assessment year 2020-21 and 2021-22 - Employer of assessee deducted tax at source from salary income of assessee for two years but did not deposit same with Government - When assessee filed return of income disclosing tax deducted at source, there was a mismatch in system and accordingly, demand was raised upon assessee by an intimation issued under section 143(1) - Whether since there was failure on part of employer to deposit tax deducted at source from salary income of assessee, revenue could not have raised any demand against assessee in view of provisions of section 205 read with Instruction No. 275 dated 01.06.2015 and Office Memorandum dated 11.03.2016 - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 10] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where employer of assessee deducted tax at source from salary income of assessee but did not deposit same with Government, Assessing Officer could not have raised any demand against assessee in view of provisions of section 205 read with CBDT's Instruction No. 275 dated 1-6-2015

Section 205, read with  section 199, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (Scope of provision) - Assessment years 2009-10, 2011-12 and 2012-13 - Employer paid salary to assessee after deduction of tax at source but did not deposit same with department - Assessing Officer did not allow credit of tax deducted at source and raised demand against assessee towards tax and interest - Whether assessee having accepted salary after deduction of tax at source had no further control over it and it was duty of employer to pay deducted tax to department and employer having failed to perform his duty to deposit deducted tax, assessee could not be penalized - Held, yes - Whether section 199 could not operate as impediment to grant relief to assessee and, thus, impugned demand deserved to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 8, 9 and 10] [In favour of assessee]   Circulars and Notifications : Instruction No. 275, dated 1-6-2015; Office Memorandum dated 11-3-2016 and Press Release, dated 11-3-2016

Section 205, read with sections 234B and 234BC, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee (TDS Credit) - Assessment year 2024-25 - Assessee, an employee, received gross salary from his employer - Employer deducted TDS from his salary but did not issue Form 16 - Assessee filed return declaring salary and claimed said TDS credit - While processing return under section 143(1), CPC denied TDS credit on ground that no corresponding TDS was available in Form 26AS and assessee failed to submit Form 16 and levied interest under sections 234B and 234C - It was noted that employer had not paid any TDS after deducting from employee and after deducting TDS neither remitted amount to Government account nor filed any quarterly returns - Further assessee was an ex-employee and, thus, was not in a position to acquire relevant document from company - Whether since assessee had brought on record relevant salary slips to demonstrate that tax was deducted from salary, revenue could not deny tax credit to assessee - Held, yes - Whether, accordingly, interest levied under sections 234B and 234C was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 6 and 7] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where employer had not given any Form 16 to assessee after deducting TDS from salary and assessee had brought on record relevant salary slips to demonstrate that tax was deducted from salary, revenue could not deny tax credit to assessee

Section 199, read with sections 234B and 234C, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted (Illustrations) - Assessment years 2018-19 and 2019-20 - During year under consideration, assessee had earned salary income - It had claimed refund of TDS deducted under section 192 - Assessing Officer denied claim of TDS to assessee on ground that same was not reflecting in Form 26AS and consequently, had charged interest under sections 234B and 234C - Whether since assessee himself acting as MD and CEO of its company did not deduct TDS on salary paid/payable to himself for working as MD and CEO of company, he could not be allowed to take benefit of his own wrong and, thus, was not entitled to any claim of set-off of TDS, which was never deposited by company - Held, yes [Paras 12 and 13] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where assessee being managing director and chief executive officer of company himself did not deduct TDS on salary paid/payable to himself for working as MD and CEO of company, he could not be allowed to take benefit of his own wrong and, thus, was not entitled to any claim of set off of TDS which was never deposited by company

Section 205 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar Against Direct Demand on Assessee (Non-deposit of TDS) - Assessment year 2020-21 and 2021-22 - Employer of assessee deducted tax at source from salary income of assessee for two years but did not deposit same with Government - When assessee filed return of income disclosing tax deducted at source, there was a mismatch in system and accordingly, demand was raised upon assessee by an intimation issued under section 143(1) - Whether since there was failure on part of employer to deposit tax deducted at source from salary income of assessee, revenue could not have raised any demand against assessee in view of provisions of section 205 read with Instruction No. 275 dated 01.06.2015 and Office Memorandum dated 11.03.2016 - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 10] [In favour of assessee]   Circulars and Notifications : Instruction No. 275, dated 1-6-2015 and Office Memorandum F. No. 275/29/2014-IT(B), dated 11-3-2016.

Section  205, read with section  143(1), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deduction of tax at source -  Bar Against Direct Demand on Assessee - Assessment years 2008-09, 2010-11, 2011-12, 2012-13 and 2013-14 - Petitioner/assessee, a former Judge of Gauhati High Court and later Upa-Lokayukta, Assam, received demand notices under section 143(1) for aforesaid financial years aggregating Rs. 8.40 lakhs on ground that credit for TDS was not reflected in Form 26AS - Petitioner submitted TDS certificates issued by Gauhati High Court and Lokayukta, Assam, and affidavits were filed by Registrar General and Registrar-cum-Secretary confirming deduction of tax from salary and deposit in Central Government Account - Department, however, declined to allow credit and insisted on payment - It was observed that law is well settled that assessee cannot be forced to pay tax which has already been deducted and deposited by deductor - Whether merely because TDS was not reflected in Form 26AS, Department could not raise demand or refuse credit and defect of non-reflection could be cured by Department in consultation with deductors - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, demand notices were to be set aside and Department was to be directed to allow credit forthwith - Held, yes [Paras 13 to 15] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where TDS was deducted from assessee's salary and was deposited in Central Government Account by Gauhati High Court, action of Department in raising demand on assessee and refusing TDS credit merely due to non-reflection in Form 26AS was unsustainable

Section 199 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at 
source - Credit for tax deducted - Assessment year 2002-03 - Assessee derived salary income from one company and professional fees from another company but those employers did not issue any tax deducted at source (TDS) certificates to assessee - However, he filed his return claiming credit of said TDS, which was disallowed by Assessing Officer - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) could not grant relief to 
assessee on ground that he could not produce evidence of TDS deduction except bank statements and some pay-slips - However, 
 Commissioner (Appeals) directed Assessing Officer to give full credit of said TDS in case, it was established on verification from TDS wing that payers actually deducted tax and filed TDS return - Whether there was no error in direction of Commissioner (Appeals) under given facts and circumstances of case - Held, yes

Section 199 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted - Assessment years 2001-02 to 2003-04 - Whether once tax is deducted on income credited by assessee in its books of account and a requisite certificate to this effect is issued by deductors after deposit of tax amount in Government treasury, assessee becomes entitled to credit of such TDS while computing tax liability for relevant period - Held, yes - Whether credit for TDS must in every case be given to assessee from whom income-tax was deducted at source and paid to credit of Central Government - Held, yes - Whether if recipient of income considers that he is not liable to tax in respect of income, wholly or partly and, therefore, does not disclose amount of such income in his return, income-tax department cannot refuse to give credit merely by contending that income had not been disclosed in return filed by assessee for assessment year - Held, yes

Section 205, read with sections 192, 199 and 203, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Collection and recovery of tax - Bar against direct demand on assessee - Assessment year 1996-97 - Whether in view of section 205, income-tax authorities, under no circumstances, can make assessee liable to make payment of any tax to extent to which tax has been deducted at source by person paying salary to assessee under section 192 - Held, yes - Whether, however, at same time, credit for tax deducted at source cannot be given to assessee unless he submits certificate as prescribed under section 203 in 
 respect of TDS as per provisions of section 199 - Held, yes - Whether till powers available to income-tax authorities to enforce payment of tax by deductor and also enforce issue of certificate in respect thereof to payee were not exercised by revenue authorities to corner deductor of tax, no tax as well as interest pertaining thereto could be recovered from assessee - Held, yes.

Section  199,  read with section  205,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deduction of tax at source  -  Credit for tax deducted  (Scope of provision) - Assessment year  2020-21  - Assessee let out his flat to a company under a leave and license agreement - Licensee deducted TDS from rent receipts but did not deposit part of it - Assessing Officer declined TDS credit to assessee to extent of shortfall on ground that same was not reflected in Form 26AS - It was noted that assessee had submitted necessary evidence like copies of ITR, computation, statement in Form 26AS, leave and license agreement, bank statement to support facts of case - Furthermore, revenue had not doubted fact that tax was deducted at source but was not deposited by deductor - Whether thus, Assessing Officer was directed to allow credit of TDS after due verification of facts on record - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of assessee]

Section  205  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deduction of tax at source  -  Bar Against Direct Demand on Assessee  (Non-deposit of TDS) - Assessment year  2020-21 and 2021-22  - Employer of assessee deducted tax at source from salary income of assessee for two years but did not deposit same with Government - When assessee filed return of income disclosing tax deducted at source, there was a mismatch in system and accordingly, demand was raised upon assessee by an intimation issued under section 143(1) - High Court held that since there was failure on part of employer to deposit tax deducted at source from salary income of assessee, revenue could not have raised any demand against assessee in view of provisions of section 205 read with  Instruction No. 275 dated 01.06.2015  and Office Memorandum dated 11.03.2016 - It was noted that common order passed by High Court had already been considered in a connected matter in Income-tax Assessing Officer, Baroda v. Shobhan Shantilal Doshi [2026] 182 taxmann.com 555 (SC), and same was disposed of by clarifying directions given with reference to changes to be made in software - Whether in view of directions already issued, no further order was required to be passed in impugned petition and, thus, SLP was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 3 and 4] [In favour of assessee]

Section  205, read with section  143(1), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deduction of tax at source -  Bar Against Direct Demand on Assessee - Assessment years 2008-09, 2010-11, 2011-12, 2012-13 and 2013-14 - Petitioner/assessee, a former Judge of Gauhati High Court and later Upa-Lokayukta, Assam, received demand notices under section 143(1) for aforesaid financial years aggregating Rs. 8.40 lakhs on ground that credit for TDS was not reflected in Form 26AS - Petitioner submitted TDS certificates issued by Gauhati High Court and Lokayukta, Assam, and affidavits were filed by Registrar General and Registrar-cum-Secretary confirming deduction of tax from salary and deposit in Central Government Account - Department, however, declined to allow credit and insisted on payment - It was observed that law is well settled that assessee cannot be forced to pay tax which has already been deducted and deposited by deductor - Whether merely because TDS was not reflected in Form 26AS, Department could not raise demand or refuse credit and defect of non-reflection could be cured by Department in consultation with deductors - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, demand notices were to be set aside and Department was to be directed to allow credit forthwith - Held, yes [Paras 13 to 15] [In favour of assessee]

Section 199 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted - Assessment year 2006-07 - Assessee was a judicial officer in State Judicial Service - For relevant assessment year, he claimed credit for tax deducted at source by employer - He also furnished form 16 but as it was self attested instead of being attested by employer, Assessing Officer did not give credit for tax deducted at source - Whether a complete machinery is provided under Act for recovery of tax deducted at source from person who has deducted such tax at source and revenue is barred from recovering such amount from person from whose income tax had been deducted at source - Held, yes - Whether assessee was a Judicial Officer in State Judicial Service and if tax was deducted at source it was most unlikely that it had not been deposited in treasury by State Government - Held, yes - Whether therefore impugned order was to be set aside and Assessing Officer was to be directed to  verify as to whether as a matter of fact, tax was deducted at source from salary of assessee and if that was so found to be correct, to grant further credit for tax, as the case may be - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]

I. Section  199,  read with section  205,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Deduction of tax at source  -  Credit for tax deducted  (Scope of) - Assessment year  2022-23  - Assessee, a law firm, received payments from its clients net of TDS, i.e., deductors withheld applicable TDS before releasing amounts - Assessee claimed credit of TDS while offering entire gross receipts to tax - However, Assessing Officer denied claim solely on ground that such amounts did not feature in Form No. 26AS - Consequently, a demand was raised comprising disallowed TDS together with interest under sections 234B and 234C - It was noted that assessee had demonstrated deduction of tax at source through its invoices and bank statements - Reconciliation placed on record showed deduction by a company which was not deposited owing to company's financial condition - Whether section 205 erects a clear bar against making a direct demand on assessee to extent tax had been deducted at source from his income and moment deduction was shown on strength of primary evidence, embargo of section 205 attaches and deductee could not again be called upon to bear burden - Held, yes - Whether since assessee had already brought corresponding income to tax, denial of credit in assessee's hands, because deductor failed to deposit or misreported deduction, would result in taxing same income twice - Held, yes - Whether thus, assessee was entitled to credit of TDS to extent deduction from its receipts was established on basis of contemporaneous material placed on record - Held, yes [Paras 19, 24 and 27] [In favour of assessee]

Section 199, read with section 144, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted (Credit of TDS) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee was an employee of Indian Railways - He had received salary income but had not filed his return of income - Accordingly, Assessing Officer passed an assessment order under section 144 and made addition to assessee's income based on salary received by assessee as reflected in Form 26AS - Assessee contended that TDS was deducted from his salary which was duly reflected in Form 26AS, therefore, matter should be remanded back to Assessing Officer for verification of facts and to allow credit of TDS - It was noted that addition in case of assessee was made by Assessing Officer based on income of assessee reflected in Form 26AS, but TDS credit available in Form 26AS was not allowed to assessee - Whether since legitimate credit of TDS was not allowed by Assessing Officer, in spite of having such facts on records, there was perversity in order of Assessing Officer and therefore, matter was to be remanded back to Assessing Officer for fresh adjudication - Held, yes [Para 8] [Matter remanded]

Section 237, read with section 243, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Refund - General (TDS credit) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Petitioner claimed refund of tax deducted at source - It was not granted by Assessing Officer on ground that there was mismatch between details furnished by assessee and details shown in Form 26 AS uploaded by deductor - However, it was found that TDS certificate were filed by assessee and deductor in instant case was a Government Department - Further, no effort was made by Assessing Officer to verify fact as to whether deductor had made payment of TDS in government account - Whether Assessing Officer was under a duty to verify whether or not deductor had made payment of TDS in government account - Held, yes - Whether there was a presumption that deductor had deposited TDS amount in government account especially when deductor was a government department - Held, yes - Whether in instant case, there was no fault on part of petitioner and fault, if any, lay with deductor - Held, yes - Whether since delay in refunding amount was attributable solely with Income Tax Department and there was no fault on part of assessee, refund was to be granted along with interest - Held, yes [Paras 11, 12 and 14][In favour of assessee]IT : Refund claim made by deductee could not be denied by Assessing Officer on ground that there was mis-match between details furnished by deductee and Form 26AS without verifying whether or not deductor had made payment of TDS in government account

Section 199, read with sections 192 and 205, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted - Assessment years 2018-19 and 2019-20 - Assessee declared its total income by filing its return of income - Assessee claimed TDS amount deducted by employer from salary - Assessing Officer disallowed claim on ground that employer of assessee had not reflected TDS in Form No. 26AS - Assessee contended that employer had not provided Form No. 16 and he was a regular defaulter - Whether assessee was required to discharge its primary onus by producing relevant documents, then only, it could claim right in its right perspective - Held, yes - Whether since assessee had failed to file any document, wherefrom it could be reflected that assessee had received any particular amount of salary on which TDS had been deducted and therefore, in absence of relevant documents, Commissioner correctly held that Assessing Officer had not made any mistake in non-granting of credit of TDS - Held, yes - Whether however, in absence of relevant documents, issue remained to be adjudicated properly and in its right perspective and therefore, for proper and just decision of case and for end of justice, it was appropriate to remand instant case to file of Commissioner for decision afresh on issue under consideration by giving reasonable opportunity to assessee to produce relevant documents - Held, yes [Paras 6.1 and 6.2] [Matter remanded]

Section 199 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted - Assessment year 1989-90 - On 29-11-1989, assessee filed loss return and claimed refund of tax paid by it which included amount of tax deducted at source under section 194A by two companies, viz., ‘L’ and ‘P’ - As ‘L’ and ‘P’ had failed to deposit TDS amount, department initiated action against them - However, on writ petition filed by ‘L’ and ‘P’, High Court permitted them to deposit TDS up to 15-4-1990 and ‘L’ and ‘P’, accordingly, deposited same on or before 15-4-1990 - Assessing Officer initially determined refund by giving credit of TDS - Subsequently, Assessing Officer withdrew credit of TDS given to assessee as TDS amount was not paid to Central Government on date of filing of return - Whether since TDS amount was already paid to Central Government, Assessing Officer was not justified in withdrawing credit of TDS given to assessee - Held, yes

Section 199, read with sections 192 and 205, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted - Assessment years 2018-19 and 2019-20 - Assessee declared its total income by filing its return of income - Assessee claimed TDS amount deducted by employer from salary - Assessing Officer disallowed claim on ground that employer of assessee had not reflected TDS in Form No. 26AS - Assessee contended that employer had not provided Form No. 16 and he was a regular defaulter - Whether assessee was required to discharge its primary onus by producing relevant documents, then only, it could claim right in its right perspective - Held, yes - Whether since assessee had failed to file any document, wherefrom it could be reflected that assessee had received any particular amount of salary on which TDS had been deducted and therefore, in absence of relevant documents, Commissioner correctly held that Assessing Officer had not made any mistake in non-granting of credit of TDS - Held, yes - Whether however, in absence of relevant documents, issue remained to be adjudicated properly and in its right perspective and therefore, for proper and just decision of case and for end of justice, it was appropriate to remand instant case to file of Commissioner for decision afresh on issue under consideration by giving reasonable opportunity to assessee to produce relevant documents - Held, yes [Paras 6.1 and 6.2] [Matter remanded]INCOME TAX : Where assessee claimed TDS amount deducted by employer from salary and Assessing Officer denied claim on ground that employer of assessee had not reflected TDS in Form 26AS, however assessee alleged that his employer had not provided him Form No. 16 and was a regular defaulter, in view of fact that assessee failed to file any document to substantiate his claim, matter was to be remanded to Commissioner for decision afresh

Section 205 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee - Assessment year 2021-22 - Petitioners were former employees of a company under investigation for financial crimes - Tax department issued demand notices against petitioners for non-deposit of TDS by their former employer - Petitioners contended that as per section 205, they could not be held liable for TDS not deposited by their employer - It was noted that object and purpose behind provision of section 205 is to effect that when an obligation to deposit tax is on employer and if employer has defaulted, liability to pay such tax cannot be shifted so as to be foisted on employee, who is in fact beneficiary of payment to be received from employer and who would also become beneficiary of tax being deposited at source on his behalf - Whether since tax department had without any warrant in law, foisted liability to pay such tax on petitioners (employees), it was clearly in breach of section 205 - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, impugned demand notices issued to petitioners were to be quashed and set aside - Held, yes [Paras 8 and 9] [In favour of assessee]

Section 205, read with section 194-I, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Bar against direct demand on assessee - Assessment year 2004-05 - Whether if tax is deductible at source under Act and has actually been deducted, assessee (deductee) cannot be called upon to pay tax in terms of provisions of section 205 - Held, yes - Assessee filed its return of income claiming refund out of amount of tax deducted at source under section 194-I - However, credit of TDS was denied in hands of assessee on ground that TDS certificates were defective inasmuch as they did not indicate date of payment of TDS to account of Central Government - Whether since TDS certificates showed that tax liable to be deducted at source was deducted, assessee was entitled to have benefit of TDS - Held, yes - Whether it was for department to recover amount of TDS from deductor and take such action against him as may be warranted, in law, but deductee could not be made to suffer for illegalities committed by deductor - Held, yes

Section 199 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted (Applicability of) - Whether where deductor having deducted TDS, issued Form No. 16A, credit of same could not be denied to assessee deductee solely on ground that such credit did not appear on ITD system of department and/or same did not match with ITD system of department - Held, yes [Para 11] [In favour of assessee]IT: Where deductor having deducted TDS, issued Form No. 16A, credit of same can not be denied to assessee deductee solely on ground that such credit does not appear on ITD system of department and/or same does not match with ITD system of department

Section 199 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted - Assessment year 2003-04 - Whether when a particular income is received by assessee after deduction of tax at source and said TDS has been duly deposited with Government and assessee has received requisite certificate to this effect, then on production of said certificate assessee becomes entitled to credit of TDS, even if assessee has not directly offered said income for tax as assessee considers that same is not liable for tax - Held, yes

Section 199 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deduction of tax at source - Credit for tax deducted (Trust) - Assessment year 2023-24 - Assessee, a sole beneficiary of private trust filed his return of income claiming credit for tax deducted at source (TDS) on income earned from trust - Assessing Officer denied TDS credit on ground that same did not appear in Form No. 26AS of assessee - Assessee submitted that since income was offered for tax in year under consideration in his hands, credit for claim of TDS should have been allowed to it - It is settled position that Department grants credit for TDS only if said amount appears in Form No. 26AS of relevant assessee - Since TDS credit in present case was not appearing in Form No. 26AS of assessee, Assessing Officer, relying strictly on procedural compliance, declined to grant such credit - Ideally, assessee ought to have ensured that deductor deducted tax in hands of assessee rather than in name of trust - However, Department has neither granted credit for TDS in hands of trust nor in hands of assessee - Whether since Commissioner (Appeals) had already directed Assessing Officer to verify assessee’s claim and grant TDS credit and if such credit had not been granted till date of passing of this order, Assessing Officer was to be directed to take necessary steps to address request of both assessee and trust for transfer of TDS credit from Form No. 26AS of trust to Form No. 26AS of assessee and, thereafter, to allow credit in accordance with law - Held, yes [Para 3.2] [Partly in favour of assessee]

facts.text:
■

The assessee was an employee of company, D. The employer had deducted TDS from monthly salary of the assessee, however, same was not deposited to the Government. The assessee filed return and claimed TDS as pre-paid taxes.

■

The Assessing Officer denied assessee's claim.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) restored the matter back to the file of the Assessing Officer directing him to verify the claim of the assessee from Form 26AS and ITR and if the claim was found to be correct, an appropriate amount of TDS credit be allowed to the assessee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee, an employee, received salary on which TDS was deducted. However, the employer had not deposited the TDS to the account of the Central Government.

■

The assessee had filed his return of income and claimed credit of the TDS that was deducted in the salary.

■

In the intimation issued, the credit of the TDS had not been granted and a demand was raised against the assessee in lieu of the credit of the TDS not granted.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee–employee filed a return declaring total income of about Rs. 70.37 lakhs for the year under consideration and claimed TDS credit of about Rs. 18.10 lakhs.

■

The return was processed under section 143(1) by CPC, which allowed TDS credit of about Rs. 0.60 lakhs only, restricting the balance claim.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the AO to grant an opportunity of being heard, verify the TDS with Form 26AS and other relevant material to ascertain whether it related to the income offered in the year, and thereafter grant credit if the claim was found correct.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal, the assessee contended that his employer had paid salary of about Rs. 57.50 lakhs and deducted TDS of about Rs. 17.50 lakhs for which credit should be allowed; the Revenue contended the employer had not deposited the deducted TDS in the Government account and, therefore, credit could not be allowed.

■

The assessee, employee, received salary after deduction of tax at source. The assessee was also issued TDS Form showing full amount of Tax Deducted at source. However, the employer company had gone into liquidation and consequently, the tax deducted was not deposited in Government account.

■

The assessee filed return claiming TDS credit.

■

The Assessing Officer raised demand onaccount of denial of TDS credit due to the mismatch with Form 26AS.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessment order.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee, a salaried employee, filed his income tax return for assessment year 2013-14, reporting a gross salary from its employer-company with TDS deducted. However, a significant discrepancy was found between the TDS amount deducted by the employer and the amount reflected in Form 26AS obtained from the Income Tax Department website.

■

Despite the tax being deducted, a portion of the amount had not been transmitted to the Income Tax Department by the employer.

■

Consequently, the assessee was deprived of receiving credit for the full TDS amount, leading to a demand notice issued by the income tax department, inclusive of interest under Sections 234B and 234C.

■

In the instant writ petition, the assessee argued that they should not be penalized for the employer's failure to fulfill this obligation. They relied on section 205, which prohibitted direct demands on the assessee, and cited circulars dated 01.06.2015 issued CBDT to support their argument.

For the assessment year 2004-05 the assessee-company had paid salary of certain sum to its non-resident employees and claimed deduction of same under section 40(a)( iii). During the course of the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer asked the assessee as to why the expenditure on account of salary be not disallowed under section 40(a)( iii). The assessee submitted before the Assessing Officer that since tax had already been paid to the credit of the Government account, no such disallowance was called for, as section 40(a)( iii) does not intend so. However, the Assessing Officer after making a reference to the provision contained in section 40(a)(iii ), and to the Circular No. 7 of 2003, dated 5-9-2003 issued by the CBDT, had taken the view that it was obligatory on the part of the assessee-company to deposit the TDS deducted on payment of salary, to the credit of the Government account by 7-4-2004, as provided under rule 30 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 and since TDS on salary was not paid within the prescribed time, such expenditure was not allowable under section 40(a)(iii ). On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed the Assessing Officer to allow the deduction inasmuch as disallowance could be made only when tax had not been paid nor had not been deducted.

On revenue's appeal :

The assessee derived salary income from a company for which he worked from October 2000 to January 2002 and also received professional fees from another company. Since assessee’s employers deducted tax at source (TDS), from such payment made by them, he claimed credit thereof in his return accordingly. The Assessing Officer, however, disallowed the same on the ground that the assessee did not possess the requisite TDS certificate. On appeal, since the assessee could not produce the evidence of TDS deduction except the bank statements and some payslips, the Commissioner (Appeals) could not grant relief to the assessee. He, however, directed the Assessing Officer to verify from the TDS wing to establish whether the payers actually deducted the tax and/or filed the TDS return or not. He was also directed to give full credit of the TDS made on the basis of such verification report in case the same was found positive. The Commissioner (Appeals) alternatively directed the Assessing Officer that in case, the credit for TDS could not be made, at least the corresponding receipts should be reduced so that only the net receipts credited in the bank account be treated as the gross receipts on which the assessee might agree to pay the taxes again.

On cross appeal :

Since 16-4-2008, the assessee was employed with Kingfisher Airlines Limited as an airlines pilot at the rank of Captain.

For the relevant assessment years the employer paid salary to the assessee after deduction of tax at source but did not deposit the same with the department.

The Assessing Officer processed under section 143(1) the return of income furnished by the assessee and did not allow the credit of tax deducted at source and raised demand against him towards tax and interest.

On writ petition :

The petitioner-assessee was a pilot by profession and was an employee of 'K' Airlines. The Airlines deducted TDS in case of assessee, however, since amount had not been deposited by the Airlines in the Central Government Account, the credit when claimed by the assessee was not given by the respondent and the demand had been raised with interest.

The assessee filed rectification applications under section 154 and asked for cancellation of demand. These were ignored and recovery notice was issued to assessee by respondent Income-tax Department.

On writ petition under article 226:

The assessee’s employer paid salary to him after deducting the tax therefrom. But despite repeated requests made by the assessee, his employer did not furnish the requisite TDS certificate. Consequently, he filed his return without Form No. 16 and also requested the Assessing Officer to enforce the issue of said certificate by the employer in exercise of his jurisdiction over the matter. However, in the absence of the same, the Assessing Officer framed the assessment under section 143(1)(a) raising tax demand in respect of salary income which was levied for the TDS certificate not furnished as well as interest payable in respect of the said tax. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that in the absence of Form No. 16 and Form No. 24, giving credit for TDS on salary did not appear to be justified, though the assessee could not be asked to pay the tax again to the extent to which tax had already been deducted in view of section 205. He, accordingly, directed the Assessing Officer to ask the assessee to obtain the same from the employer and furnish the same.

On second appeal :

■

The assessee-pilot by profession, was an employee of Kingfisher Airlines. During the relevant assessment years, Kingfisher Airlines (deductor) had deducted TDS on assessee's salary but the same was not deposited by the deductor in the Central Government Account.

■

The assessee filed return and claimed credit for TDS.

■

However, the Assessing Officer did not grant credit due to mismatch of TDS and raised demand along with interest.

■

Thereafter, the assessee received intimation under Section 245 proposing adjustment of refund against the outstanding demand.

■

On writ :

■

The assessee was an employee of Kingfisher Airlines.

■

Kingfisher Airlines deducted TDS from salary of assessee but did not deposit same with Government.

■

The Assessing Officer disallowed the amount of TDS and raised a demand against the assessee.

■

On writ petition, the assessee contended that the respondent had recovered the substantial amount of said demand from the amount of refund which became due to the assessee.

■

The assessee-employee filed its return claiming TDS amounting to Rs.10.45 lakhs which was deducted by employer from salary under section 192,

■

The Assessing Officer denied claim on the ground that the employer of the assessee had not reflected the TDS in Form No. 26AS.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal :

In his return of income for the relevant assessment year 1997-98, the assessee claimed credit of the tax deducted at source by his employer. According to him, the tax had been deducted by the employer every time the payment of salary was made to him, but the employer had not furnished Form No. 16 or any other relevant evidence to prove that the tax had been deducted from his salary. The assessee filed copies of the pay slips for two months to show that income-tax was deducted from those payments and as per the assessee, it was a prima facie evidence to show that the former employer had been deducting income-tax from his salary. However, the Assessing Officer was not satisfied with the said evidence. He, thus, rejected the assessee's claim of credit of tax on ground that in the absence of a statutory certificate, credit of TDS could not be given.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

The assessee had sold a property to a purchaser for a consideration of certain amount who deducted TDS at the rate of 1 per cent of the sale consideration amount as per the provisions of section 194-IA as the consideration was in excess of Rs.50 lakhs and paid balance amount to the assessee. However, the vendee had not deposited the TDS deducted in Government's account and had not given the required Form 16B for deduction of tax at source to the assessee. The assessee filed return and claimed credit of said TDS amount. However same was disallowed by CPC for reason that TDS deducted was not deposited.

The Commissioner (Appeals)-NFAC also upheld order of CPC.

The assessee filed on instant appeal to the Tribunal and contended that once purchaser of property had deducted tax at source out of payments due/paid to the assessee, but had not deposited tax withheld by it, the assessee should not suffer and credit TDS should be allowed to it.

During the financial year 1988-89 relevant to assessment year 1989-90, two companies namely L and P had paid interest due to the assessee after deducting tax at source. On 29-11-1989, the assessee filed loss return and claimed refund of tax paid by it which, inter alia, included the amount of tax deducted at source under section 194A by two companies viz. ‘L’ and ‘P’. ‘L’ and ‘P’ had failed to deposit the TDS amount deducted from the income of the assessee with the Department within the time prescribed and, therefore, the income-tax authorities initiated action against them. However, on writ petition, the High Court permitted them to deposit the TDS amount with the Department in instalment up to 15-4-1990 and both the companies had deposited the TDS amount in the Government treasury on or before 15-4-1990. The Assessing Officer, by intimation under section 143(1)(a) made prima facie adjustments such as additional tax under section 143(1A) to the loss return filed by the assessee and after giving credit of pre-paid tax which included sum being tax deducted at source by the aforesaid two companies and adjusting the TDS liability, determined the refund payable to the assessee and interest under section 244A. Subsequently, the Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 154 calling upon the assessee to show cause as to why the intimation should not be rectified by withdrawing the credit of TDS given to the assessee as the TDS amounts were in fact not paid to the Central Government by the said companies on the date on which the return of income was filed by the assessee. The assessee contended that the said two companies had paid the TDS amount to the Department within the time allowed by the High Court and under section 205, the income-tax authorities could not demand the TDS amount from the assessee for the failure of the said companies, which deducted the tax, to pay to the Central Government and, accordingly, the credit for the TDS amount with interest granted under section 244A could not be withdrawn. Rejecting the contention of the assessee, the Assessing Officer passed the rectification order under section 154 thereby withdrawing the credit of TDS as well as the interest amount granted under section 244A and raised a demand. Thereafter, the Assessing Officer adjusted the said demand against refund payable to the assessee for next assessment year.

Respondent No. 6 company appointed the assessee as managing director with effect from 1-4-1996. During the period April to December 1996, respondent No. 6 paid certain amount of salary to the assessee after deducting TDS. Thereafter, dispute arose between the parties and ultimately respondent No. 6 terminated the services of the assessee in March 1997. On 30-9-1997, the assessee filed return of income for the assessment year 1997-98, inter alia, claiming credit of TDS. The return was processed and the Assessing Officer issued intimation under section 143(1)(a) denying credit of the TDS amount. Thereafter, the Assessing Officer raised a demand of TDS along with interest under sections 234A, 234B and 234C. The assessee then wrote various letters to the revenue to recover the TDS amount collected by respondent No. 6 and to compel it to issue TDS certificate in favour of the assessee. Instead of recovering the amount from respondent No. 6, the authorities initiated penalty proceedings under section 221(1) against the assessee and attached the bank account of the assessee for recovery of the tax amount along with the interest.

On writ :

■

The assessee was employed with TLPL. The employer i.e. TLPL had paid gross salary to the assessee during the year April 2023 to August 23 and deducted TDS under section 192 but the TLPL did not provide any Form 16 to the assessee for the same period.

■

The assessee declared the gross salary income for filing the return of income and claimed the above said TDS. While processing the return under section 143(1), since there was no TDS credit against the above said salary, the TDS was denied to the assessee.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the appeal filed by the assessee by observing that the assessee had not submitted Form 16 issued by the employer and the same was also not reflected in Form 26AS.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■

The assessee was employed by 'K' Airlines Limited as a pilot from November 2008 to July 2010. During the financial years 2008-09 and 2010-11, the employer deducted tax at source out of the salary of the assessee but failed to deposit the same with the Income-tax Authorities.

■

The assessee filed return of income for assessment year 2009-10 declaring its income claiming the credit of TDS which the employer deducted from the salary. However, since the employer did not deposit the same with Income-tax Authorities, the return of income filed by the assessee was processed under section 143(1) by Jurisdictional Assessing Officer without giving credit for the same and raising demand of Rs. 11.42 lakhs.

■

The assessee filed return of income for subsequent period and the same were processed under section 143(1). In the event of the refund due to the assessee, the same was adjusted against the demand of assessment years 2009-10 or 2010-11.

■

Meanwhile the assessee filed an application for rectification under section 154 against the demand raised in the intimation for assessment year 2009-10 and adjustment of refunds of subsequent years. The Jurisdictional Assessing Officer passed an order rejecting the rectification application which was assailed before Commissioner (Appeals) who directed the Jurisdictional Assessing Officer to rectify the mistake apparent on record by verifying the contention of the assessee.

■

For long time, no order giving effect to the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was passed. The assessee thereafter requested the Jurisdictional Assessing Officer to give appeal effect of the said order.

■

Thereafter, the assessee received intimation under section 245 via E-mail proposing to adjust the refund of assessment year 2023-24 against the outstanding demand of assessment years 2009-10 and 2011-12.

■

On writ:

■

The petitioners/assessees were employees of respondent no.2. They were being paid monthly emoluments/salary, after deduction of TDS (taxes at source) by respondent No.2. Since the year 2019, respondent No.2 was involved in criminal proceedings initiated against it by the Enforcement Directorate (ED), in regard to the financial crimes. There was an investigation undertaken by SEBI on investors grievances in relation to violation of the securities law. During the course of such investigation, the directors of respondent no.2 as also some senior officers of respondent no.2 were arrested. As a consequence of these irregularities, there were defaults on the part of respondent no.2 in the payment of petitioners’ salary. Some of the employees did not at all receive their salaries while some others received delayed payments. Subsequently, the petitioners received from department the impugned notices demanding payment of income tax alongwith interest, on account of non-deposit of TDS amount by respondent no.2, which according to the petitioners, were shown to have been deducted from the salary slips as issued to the petitioners.

■

In instant writ petition to the High Court the petitioners contended that it was not permissible for department to issue such demand notices against the petitioners in view of clear provisions of section 205 of the Income Tax Act, which bars any demand against the assessees. The provision ordained that where tax is deductible at source under the provisions of Chapter XVII, the assessee should not be called upon to pay tax himself to the extent to which the tax had been deducted from the income. In this view of the matter, the petitioners submitted that no demand could had been foisted by department on the petitioners. To this effect, the petitioners had also made representations on the portal of the department that the demand might be withdrawn. However, the same had not been acted upon and the demand was stated to have subsisted.

■

The assessee had let out his ownership flat to a company under a leave and license agreement. The assessee received the license fee after deduction of the tax from licensee. The licensee had deducted TDS of Rs. 1.48 lakhs but deposited only about Rs. 0.36 lakhs.

■

The Assessing Officer declined TDS credit to assessee to the extent of the shortfall of Rs. 1.12 lakhs on ground that samewas not reflected in Form 26AS.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the claim of assessee, stating that the dispute needed to be settled between the Licensee and Licensor, thus the assessee was liable to pay legitimate taxes even if it was on account of failure of the deductor / licensee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

For the assessment year 1993-94, i.e., during the financial year 1992-93, the assessee had paid salaries to its employees and had deducted tax at source on the basis of estimated incomes of the respective employees. In the course of survey proceedings, it was observed that the assessee had allowed exemption of leave travel allowance (LTA) without verifying the actual incurrence of the expenditure as required by the provisions of section 10(5), read with rule 2B of the Income-tax Rules, 1962, and had reimbursed drivers’ salary to some of the employees but the same had not been valued at cost while considering its perquisite value. According to the ITO, the assessee had committed default within the meaning of section 201. The assessee contended that it had acted upon the declaration from the employees with regard to the details of the travel and in respect of reimbursement of drivers’ salary, the assessee relied upon rule 3(c)( ii). The ITO, however, passed an order under section 201 directing the company to pay the tax which was short deducted. The Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the assessee’s appeal.

On second appeal, the assessee contended that even if there was a shortfall in deduction of tax, conditions necessary for the applicability of section 201(1) and 201(1A) did not apply and in view of section 191, tax could not be recovered from the employer-company and that under the section, in any case, where income-tax has not been deducted, it shall be payable by assessee-employee directly.

■

The assessee, law firm, was engaged in providing legal services. The assessee received payments from clients which were net of tax deducted at source, the deductors having withheld the applicable TDS before releasing amounts. The assessee while filing return claimed credit for such deductions while offering the entire gross receipts to tax.

■

The Assessing Officer denied credit of TDS solely on the ground that such amounts did not feature in Form No. 26AS. Consequently, a demand was raised comprising the disallowed TDS together with interest under section 234B and under section 234C.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the denial of credit, holding that unless the deduction appeared in Form 26AS, the assessee could not be allowed relief. As regards levy of interest under sections 234B and 234C, the Commissioner (Appeals) held the same to be consequential and mandatory.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee provided services to a company known as Clutch Auto Ltd. (CAL), and made payment with the total value of the services amounting to Rs. 8,50,26,199. CAL, as the deductor, deducted tax at source from the payments made to the assessee, totalling Rs. 24,96,199. The assessee claimed that CAL did not fully deposit the deducted tax with the revenue department. Additionally, the assessee alleged that the balance amount, after tax deduction, was not remitted to them by CAL, and this issue was under consideration at the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT). According to the assessee, CAL only deposited Rs. 69,897 as tax deducted at source, leaving a deficit of Rs. 24,26,302. This aspect was not disputed by the revenue department. The assessee's grievance was that they were not given credit for the tax deducted at source by CAL, which was not deposited with the revenue.

Consequently, a demand of Rs. 15,24,840 was raised against the assessee.

The assessee sought a writ of mandamus or other appropriate directives to compel the revenue department to refund the amount of Rs. 11,39,870 due to them for the assessment year 2011-12.

The High Court relied on the decision of in the case of Sanjay Sudan v. Asstt. CIT [2023] 148 taxmann.com 329/292 Taxman 138/452 ITR 107 (Delhi), and concluded that the revenue department could not indirectly recover tax that could not be directly collected from the deductee, as this would contravene section 205. Consequently, by an order dated 31-5-2023 the court ordered the revenue department to refund the sum of Rs. 11,39,870 to the assessee.

The revenue, filed review application and sought for review of order dated 31-5-2023 by contending that Form 16A was not produced as evidence of tax deduction.

■

The assessees were salaried employees of ASPL. Tax at source (TDS) was deducted from their salaries but was not remitted by the employer to the Income Tax Department.

■

Due to such non-remittance, the assessee’s faced tax demands.

■

In the instant writ, the assessees contended that they should not be liable for TDS not deposited by the employer.

The assessee-company had six expatriate (contract) employees during the financial year relevant to the assessment year 1970-71, to whom the assessee paid certain tax-free salary and the employer had to pay tax on such amount of tax-free salary. It was observed from the statement filed by the assessee that although these contract employees were paid net amount of salary at a uniform monthly rate, the deposit of tax on account of this salary had not been uniform, particularly in the last two months. Thus, the employer had failed to comply with the relevant provisions of sections 192 and 200 read with the relevant provisions of the rules thereunder. The ITO charged interest under section 201(1 A) on 31-3-1976, which was set aside by the Tribunal with a direction to pass a fresh order. Consequently, the ITO passed another order on 1-6-1979 charging interest under section 201(1A). On appeal, the AAC, however, set aside the ITO's order but, on further appeal, the Tribunal restored the ITO's order.

On reference, the assessee, inter alia, contended (i) that at the time of payment of salary the company was under a legal obligation to deduct income-tax on the amounts payable to the employees and the amount payable in this case was the amount of tax -free salary and the element of tax could not be included as a part of the salary paid to the employee, (ii) that in any event, the employer being a company, it was under no obligation to deduct tax at source from the salary of an employee and the person who actually handed over the salary to the employee was the person who should have deducted the tax and any proceedings for levy of penalty or imposition of interest could only be initiated against such person who was responsible for making the payment, and (iii) that the proceeding for the recovery of the interest was barred by limitation as prescribed in section231.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) did not accept the contention of the assessee about lack of jurisdiction with the ITO (TDS) on the ground that there was a failure on the part of the employer to deduct tax in accordance with the provisions of the Act. On second appeal :

held.text:
The case is no longer res integra and is covered by the decision of this very Court rendered in case of Devarsh Pravinbhai Patel v. Asstt. CIT [R/SCA No. 12965 of 2018, dated 24-9-2018] where too, the petitioner was an employee of the Kingfisher Airlines and worked as a pilot. In his case also the TDS on the salary made to the petitioner had not been deposited. It is only when the department raised the tax demand with interest and initiated the actions of the recovery that this Court was approached. Relying on the decision of the Gauhati High Court rendered in case of Asstt. CIT v. Om Prakash Gattani [2001] 117 Taxman 549/[2000] 242 ITR 638, this Court allowed the same by holding that the petitioner-assessee deductee is entitled to credit of the tax deducted at source with respect to amount of TDS for which Form No. 16A issued by the employer deductor has been produced and consequently department is directed to give credit of tax deducted at source to the petitioner-assessee - deductee to the extent Form No. 16 A issued by the deductor have been issued. Consequently, the impugned demand notice is quashed and set aside. However, it is clarified and observed that if the department is of the opinion deductor has not deposited the said amount of tax deducted at source, it will always been open for the department to recover the same from the deductor. Thus, it is held that the Department cannot deny the benefit of tax deducted at source by the employer of the petitioner during the relevant financial years. Credit of such tax would be given to the petitioner for the respective years. If there has been any recovery or adjustment out of the refunds of the later years, the same shall be returned to the petitioner with statutory interest. [Para 7]

In case of Om Prakash Gattani (supra) Gauhati High Court was dealing with the TDS not deposited of prize money payable to the petitioner. It held and observed that a perusal of section 205 clarifies the position where it provides that where tax is deductible at source, the assessee shall not be called upon to pay the tax himself to the extent to which tax has been deducted from that income. What is noticeable in this provision is that its applicability is not dependent upon the credit for tax deducted being given under section 199. What is necessary for applicability of this provision is that the amount has been deducted from the income. In case where the amount has been deducted but not paid to the Central Government that eventuality is taken care of by section 201.The appellant could not show that under the law it maybe permissible to proceed against the assessee even after deduction of the tax at source, nor could it be held that merely by deduction of tax at source, credit for deduction of tax at source has to be given even though the amount may not have been made over to the Government treasury. As the mere deduction of tax at source would not close the chapter of tax liability unless it is deposited in the Government treasury. [Para 8]

The facts being almost identical, no separate reasoning are desirable and the petition is being allowed. The department is precluded from denying the benefit of the tax deducted at source by the employer during the relevant financial years to the petitioner. [Para 9]

The credit of the tax shall be given to the petitioner and if in the interregnum any recovery or adjustment is made by the respondent, the petitioner shall be entitled to the refund of the same, with the statutory interest, from the date of receipt of copy of this order. [Para 11]

Petition is accordingly disposed of. [Para 12]

■

The brief facts show that assessee is an employee of D. From the verification of the salary slips, it is apparent that tax is deducted from the salary of the employee by the employer. The employer has not deposited the tax to the credit of the Central Govt. Due to this, there was no credit appearing in Form 26AS of the assessee. Due to this, credit was denied by the Assessing Officer. [Para 7]

■

On appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals), direction was given to the Assessing Officer to give credit to the assessee of the TDS to the assessee if it appears in Form 26AS. Naturally when no tax is deposited by the employer after deducting tax from the salary of the employee, it will not appear in Form 26AS of employee. If the employer after deducting the tax does not deposit the same to the credit of the Central Govt., that cannot be a cause for denying the credit to the employee who has suffered the TDS by employer and the employer did not pay the tax. In fact TDS is an onerous responsibility cast upon the payer on behalf of the Govt. of India. In this case, the employer had already admitted to CIRP proceedings by order of NCLT under section 9 of IBC, 2016 vide order dated 6-8-2025. Therefore there is a moratorium available to the employer. However, the provisions of the penalty and prosecution against the responsible officer are still applicable in this case. In spite of all this, nothing is done by revenue. Assessee-employee cannot be denied the credit of taxes, when by filing the conclusive evidence, tax is deducted by the employer. [Para 8]

■

Accordingly, the Assessing Officer is directed to grant credit of the above TDS to the assessee within 60 days from the date of receipt of this order. [Para 10]

■

The Income Tax Department can give credit of TDS only to the extent of receipt. This is clear from a reading of section 199. The Gauhati High Court in CIT v. Om Praksh Gattani [2001] 117 Taxman 549/242 ITR 638 (Gauhati) that while recovery to the extent of deduction may not be possible against the assessee from whose income such tax has been deducted, the assessee cannot also straight away claim credit of the tax so deducted but not paid over to the Central Government by the deductor. This also seems to be the view taken by the Division Bench of the Bombay High Court in Aslam Checkar v. ITO [Writ Petition (L) No. 2442 of 2024, dated 10-9-2024]. It is the admitted case of the petitioners that the amounts deducted as TDS have not been remitted by the employer to the Central Government/Income Tax Department. Therefore, the petitioners cannot be granted the relief of a direction to the Income Tax Department to grant credit to the extent of tax deducted from their salaries by the entity in which they were working. They are also not entitled to a writ directing the Income Tax Department to cancel the demands pending against them even though the amounts (TDS) have not been remitted to the Central Government/Income Tax Department. This is the only way in which sections 199 and 205 can be harmoniously interpreted. The section heading of section 205 uses the words ‘direct demand on assessee’ indicating that the provision only bars recovery from the assessee and does not mandate the grant of a credit. This may raise a legitimate question - is not the denial of credit a recovery. Denial of credit may ultimately result in a recovery, if the proceedings against the de`1ductor under section 201 do not end in recovery. However, this does not lead me to give any other meaning to section 205. Accordingly, disagreement is recorded with the view taken by the Delhi High Court in Sanjay Sudan v. Asstt.. CIT [2023] 148 taxmann.com 329/292 Taxman 138/ 452 ITR 107 (Delhi), to the extent it holds that on deduction credit is immediately available to an assessee from whose income such deduction has been made even if such amount has not been paid over to the Central Government/Income Tax Department by the deductor. The instructions contained in the Office Memorandum (F.No.275/29/2014-IT(B) dated 11-3-2015) only deal with the aspect of initiation of recovery proceedings against a person from whose income a tax deduction has been made and does not deal with the question as to whether credit of such unpaid amounts of TDS has to be given to such person. [Para 5]

■

Therefore, these writ petitions will stand disposed of holding that the petitioners are not entitled to the credit of any amount of TDS deducted from their salaries but not paid over to the Income Tax Department by the entity in which they were working. The petitioners are also not entitled to a writ directing the Income Tax Department to cancel the demands pending against them even though the amounts (TDS) have not been remitted to the Central Government/Income Tax Department. It will be open to the Income Tax Department to proceed against the entity for non-payment of TDS deducted from the salaries of the petitioners by treating the entity as an assessee in default under section 201. If any amount is paid by the entity or recovered from it, credit to the extent of such payment/recovery shall be given to the petitioners in these cases and demands to the extent of such recovery will be effaced. [Para 6]

■

It is observed that the Co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in Aditya Deepak Nasta v. Section 205 is to the effect that assessee shall not be called upon to pay the tax himself to the extent to which tax has been deducted from that income. Its applicability is not dependent upon the credit for tax deducted being given under section 199. [Para 11]

The Assessing Officer shall not deny the benefit of tax deducted at source by the employer during the relevant assessment years to the assessee.
