26. Deductibility of discount given on ESOPs

Some of recent judicial pronouncements suggest that the tax fraternity is grappling with the controversy on the tax treatment of the discounts on the shares issued to the employees under ESOPs.

The revenue has been contending that the said discounts can never be allowed as deductions on the following grounds:

(a)

The discount offered under ESOP is not in the nature of expenditure;

(b)

Such discount is not given in the normal course of business carried on by the Company;

(c)

Such discount merely represents short receipt of premium on issue of shares. If the receipt of premium is not taxable, the short receipt of such premium should also not be allowed as deduction;

(d)

At the most, such discount could be considered as a short capital receipt or a sort of capital expenditure.

Conversely, the Companies issuing ESOP's argue that the primary object of an ESOP is not to raise share capital but to earn profit by securing the consistent and concentrated efforts of its dedicated employees during the vesting period. Therefore, such discount should be construed as nothing but a part of remuneration. Such discounted premium on shares is a substitute for giving direct incentive in cash for availing of the services of the employees.

In order to avoid unnecessary litigations, it would be prudent for the Finance Minister to clarify this stand on the tax treatment of discounts on issue of shares under ESOP. The industry expects a clarification stating that the discounts on ESOP scheme should be amortized over the vesting period.

Recently, In the case of Amitabh Roy v Master Development Management (India) (P.) Ltd., Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 274 of 2022, decided on 18-5-2022, the tribunal clarified that the provisions of IBC cannot be used for giving effect to the recovery of TDS amount. The appeal was presented by an ex-director of CD against the order of the adjudicating authority, which admitted an application filed by the Operational Creditor. This blog is an analysis of the whole situation in light of the relevant sections of the applicable laws.

Factual Background:

The OC preferred a Section 9 application, but the parties entered into a settlement. An order was passed to the effect by the Adjudicating Authority, that in case of the settlement fails, the application could be revived. The CD and OC entered into certain settlements and it explicitly conveyed that the amounts were inclusive of the TDS amount. The amounts were paid by the CD, and the OC prayed the revival of section 9 to the Adjudicating Authority, and an order was passed asking the CD to indicate the details of the payment. Via a supplementary affidavit, the appellants conveyed to the adjudicating authority that a certain amount of TDS remained outstanding. After this, the Adjudicating Authority admitted the application under Section 9 IBC and it is in this order the appeal has been preferred.

Observations and Decision:

The tribunal observed that there was no event or scope of failure of settlement talks between the parties and thus the intervention of Adjudicating Authority wasn't needed and made an order of revival approval. The only outstanding amount payable were the two TDS amounts. The tribunal held that non-payment of the TDS amount was no occasion for admitting application under Section 9 by the Adjudicating Authority. Taking actions against the non-payment of TDS is provided under Income Tax Act, 1961 and it is in the domain of income tax authorities. The appeal was allowed with a cost of Rupees One lakh on the Operational Creditors for misusing the process under IBC. This order has given wide scope for analysis and scope of the applicability of Section 9 IBC.

DEFAULT UNDER IBC

The event which triggers the applicability of the Code is "Occurrence of Default". And therefore, it is necessary to know what actually constitutes a "Default". A default is defined under Section 3(12) of the IBC, which defines 'default' as non-payment of debt when whole or any part or installment of the amount of debt has become due and payable and is not repaid by the debtor or the corporate debtor, as the case may be. In the case of Krishna Kilaru v. Maytas Properties Ltd. [2013] 36 taxmann.com 24 (AP.), it was observed thatthe phrase 'debt has become due and payable' means that the debt is payable at the present moment. As per the contract between the parties wherever the debt is payable after a certain point of time or on happening of a certain event, the debt becomes due only after that point of time. And if the case arises where the debt is payable and the person has not made it, a "default" is said to occur and an application for it can be brought. Another question in this regard is how to determine the default or the non-payment? WHAT IS TDS?

The concept of TDS was introduced with the aim to collect tax from the very source. According to the concept, a person liable to make payment i.e. Deductor of any specified nature to any other person i.e. the deductee shall deduct the tax at the source and remit the same in the account of the central government. And on the basis of Form 26AS or TDS certificate issued by the deductor, the deductee whose income tax has been deducted at the source would be entitled to get a credit amount so deducted. Failing to fill the TDS on time all the companies, private, or government must bear a penalty of RS.200/day, under Section 234E. However, the penalty will not increase the amount of the TDS needed to be paid. Under Section 271H, a penalty ranging from 10,000 to Rs, 1 Lakh is leviable if the company provides incorrect information or fails to submit the returns within the specified due date.

A portion of employees' salary is required to be withheld by the employers by way of contribution to Provident Fund (PF), Employees' State Insurance Corporation (ESIC) or any other superannuation fund.

The employers are entrusted with the responsibility to deposit the said contributions with the concerned Departments of Central Government of India (CG)- PF/ ESIC etc. In this regard, CG has enacted respective legislatures specifying the date of deposit contribution to be made by employers- either in respect of employer's own share towards PF / ESIC or the share which has been deducted from the salary of employee.

However, it has been observed that employers habitually delay in depositing employees' share of contributions to the concerned fund, which they have withheld from the salary of employees. This matter has witnessed substantial litigation and the Courts have given conflicting rulings - some in favor of the employers stating that employees share even if paid before the due date of filing of return of income can be claimed a deduction, while some rulings have held that deposit of employee's share of contribution made beyond the dates prescribed under the respective legislation would not be allowed as a deduction.

The Supreme Court of India in the case of Rajasthan State Beverages Corporation [2017] 84 taxmann.com 185 (SC) decided the underlying case in favor of the employers by dismissing the SLP filed against the order of Rajasthan High Court by the Department. However, very recently, after the said Supreme Court judgement, Kerala High Court in the case of M/s Popular Vehicles and Services Private Limited [2018] 96 taxmann.com 13 (Kerala) have rejected the employer's claim for deduction, if paid beyond the due date on the ground that the intent of introduction of section 36(1)(va) was to ensure that employers should not sit on the contributions collected from the employees' salary and deprive the workmen of the rightful benefits under the social welfare legislations, by delaying payment of contributions to the welfare funds. This aspect was not discussed by the Supreme Court in the case of Rajasthan State Beverages Corporation (supra) while dismissing the Revenue's SLP.

In light of the said judgement, below is a detailed discussion on the controversy of deductibility of employee's contribution in the hands of employer under section 43B.

Introduction

Allowability of deduction to the employer, towards deposit of employee's contribution to Provident Fund (PF) and Employee State Insurance (ESI) after the due dates under the respective laws but prior to the due date for filing of Income tax return under section 43B of the Income-tax Act, 1956 (the Act) has been a subject matter of constant deliberation and discussions by various Courts in the past. Courts at various junctures have analyzed this issue. Below is a brief discussion on the said issue.

Provisions under the Act

Prior to the promulgation of the Finance Act, 1987, an employer was entitled to deduction in respect of employee's share under section 36(1)(iv) & (v) of the amounts contributed by the employer towards provident fund, ESI and other superannuation schemes.

By the Finance Act of 1987, in order to penalize the employers who mis-utilize contributions to PF or any fund set up under the provisions of the ESI Act or any other fund for the welfare of employees, section 2 (24)(x) was inserted and the sums collected by the assessee from his employees as contributions to provident funds or ESI, were to be treated as income.

By the same Act, section 36(1)(va) was introduced wherein the contribution of the employees collected by the employer was allowed as deductible expense if deposited within a particular time prescribed under the relevant fund laws.

The relevant provisions of the Act are provided below:

Section 2(24)(x)

Section 2(24)(x) of the Act provides that any sum received by the employer from his employees as contribution to any provident fund or superannuation fund or any fund set up under the provisions of ESI Act or any other fund for the welfare of such employees shall be treated as employer's income.

Section 36(1)(va)

Section 36(1)(va) of the Act provides that deduction of employee's contribution towards provident fund (PF), superannuation fund or Employee State Insurance (ESI) or other employee funds, shall be allowed to the employer, provided such amount is credited to the employee's account in the relevant fund or funds on or before the 'due date' as prescribed under the relevant labour law legislations.

Explanation to the subject section defines the term 'due date' as the date by which the assessee is required as an employer to credit the employee's contribution to the employee's account in the relevant fund. So in case of PF and ESI fund, the due date is the date as provided under the PF and ESI Acts.

30. Time limit to pass an order under Section 201(3) if the assessee fails to deposit TDS

Section 201(3) of the Act prescribes the time limit for the Assessing Officer to pass an order deeming a person to be an assessee-in-default for failure to deduct the tax from a person resident in India. Controversy

The controversy with respect to deductibility of employee's contribution to welfare funds require the following issues for consideration:

Section 36(1)(va) of the Act is a specific provision enacted with an intent to take care that employees' share, deducted from salary, is deposited with the labour laws fund within prescribed dates specified in the legislature and that there is no unjust enrichment in the hands of the employers on account of such non deposit of employee's contribution.

By reading the conditions of section 36(1)(va) as having been satisfied upon deposit of employee contribution before due date of filing of return of income- and putting the same at par with due date for employer contribution under section 43B, would make section 36(1)(va) redundant by the virtue of non-obstante clause contained in section 43B of the Act.

Whether clause (2) of section 43B covers only employer's contribution or employee's contribution as well within its purview?

The above-mentioned issues have however not been dealt by either the Supreme Court and neither by the Rajasthan High Court while pronouncing the ruling in case of Rajasthan State Beverages Corporation Limited [2017] 84 taxmann.com 185 (SC) and [2017] 84 taxmann.com 173 (Rajasthan) respectively. The Court in the said orders did not consider the issue in relation to redundancy of section 36(1)(va) at all.

However, the Kerala High Court in a recent case of Popular Vehicles and Services Private Limited[TS-378-HC-2018 (Ker.)]have analyzed this issue in detail. The said Court with respect to the subject issue noticed the fact that section 43B contains a non-obstante clause cannot render otiose the Explanation to section 36(1)(va) due to the following reasons:

Section 43B, though a non-obstante clause, makes deductions to be allowable only on actual payment, when such deductions are otherwise allowable;

The non-obstante clause has no effect insofar as the employee's contribution which is specifically covered by sub-clause (va) of Section 36(1). By virtue of the specific Explanation below sub-clause (va), no deduction can be claimed if the contribution has not been paid after collection from the employees by way of deduction from their salaries, within the due date under the respective labour Laws.

Primarily, section 43B is a restrictive provision, the amendments to it or the deletion of a proviso in it cannot lead to it being converted as an enabling provision permitting deduction even when there was no deduction permissible by the other provisions of the Act;

Employee's contribution though remitted to the fund by the employer, it is deducted from the employee's salary;

Mere remittance of employee's contribution by the employer does not change the essential nature of the contribution which is of employee;

Support on this regard was taken from an observation of Supreme Court in the case of Alom Extrusions that the employer should not sit on the collected contributions and deprive workmen of the rightful benefits under social welfare legislations by delaying payment of contributions to the welfare funds.

The Court also analysed the principle of 'Albeit an illegal enrichment' and held that if the employee's contribution which the employer deducts from his salary is not remitted into the fund on or before the due date under the respective Acts, the employer not only has defaulted the stipulation in the labour legislation but has received an income.

Based on the above stated observations, the Court held that employee's contribution is outside the purview of section 43B.

SERVICE TAX — RATE OF INTEREST

1. Please explain the term 'Service tax collected but not paid' for the purposes of calculating interest liability under service tax law, as per notifications forming part of the Budget 2016-17. Would it cover : (a) service tax due on the basis of invoice but not actually received, or (b) service tax actually received.

Sections 73B and 75 of the Finance Act, 1994 are amended to empower Government to notify different rate of interest in cases where service tax has been collected and not paid. After enactment of Bill, rate of interest under Section 73B (sum collected in name of service tax but not paid) would be 15% [Notification No. 8/2006-ST, as amended] and that under Section 75 would be 15% (24% when service tax is collected but not paid on due date) [Notification 13/2016-ST].

The language used for rate of interest of 24% is : "Collection of any amount as service tax but failing to pay the amount so collected to the credit of the Central Government on or before the date on which such payment becomes due."

The word "collection" would refer to actual collection and not merely billing. In that view of the matter, the rate of interest of 24% would apply only if service tax has been billed and "actually collected" from the service recipient but not paid.

Note : There is no intelligible differentia between section 73B (sum collected in name of service tax but not paid) and section 75 (service tax collected but not paid) and therefore, rate of interest should be same. We should expect challenge on count of discrimination/arbitrariness, as section 73B reflects greater offence. The government should modify rate of interest under Section 73B to be 24%.

7. Higher rate of interest for non-deposit of TCS amount

Section 201 provides the consequences in case of any failure to deduct or to pay the tax deducted at source. The Section provides that deductor shall be liable to pay interest at the rate of 1% per month/part of the month in case there is a failure to deduct tax. However, where deduction has been made but tax has not been deposited, the interest is levied at the rate of 1.5% for every month or part of the month.

In contrast to above, section 206C which specifically deals with, the consequences of failure to collect or to pay tax collected at source (TCS), levies only a single rate of interest. If the collector fails to collect TCS or after collecting fails to deposit it with Govt., interest is levied at the rate of 1% for every month or part month.

It is expected that the Govt. may bring parity in the penal provision for both the default. Section 206C could be amended to provide a higher rate of interest in case tax has been collected but not deposited to the credit of Central Govt.

8. Retrospective applicability of Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016

The Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 was amended by the Benami Transaction (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016 (hereinafter referred to as Amendment Act). It came into force with effect from 01-11-2016. By the Amendment Act, the Govt. has redefined and widened the provisions of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988. The Amendment Act had introduced extensive provisions on definitions, authorities, attachment, adjudication and confiscation, etc. whereas the original Act had just nine sections.

After the enactment of the Amendment Act, 2016, the Initiating Officers started issuing notices for provisional attachment of the alleged Benami properties which were challenged on the ground that the provisions of Amendment Act, 2016 could not be applied with retrospective effect. Thus, properties purchased before 01-01-2016 shall be out of the ambit of Benami law.

So far we have witnessed multiple High Courts' rulings on this issue. The Calcutta High Court in the case of Ganpati Dealcom (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 112 taxmann.com 367 (Calcutta)had held that the Amendment Act was new legislation and to have effect retrospectively it should have been explicitly provided therein that it was intended to cover contraventions at an earlier point of time. That express provision is not there and thus the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016 could not be applied retrospectively.

However, the Chhattisgarh court in the case of Tulsiram v. ACIT [2019] 112 taxmann.com 129 (Chhattisgarh)had ruled in the favour of revenue and held that the Prohibitions of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988 as it stands today, after incorporating the effect of Amendment Act that brought into force with effect from 1-11-2016, shall apply irrespective of period of purchase of alleged Benami property.

Considering the ongoing disputes in this matter and to avoid any further litigations, it is expected that Govt. could clarify the applicability of the Benami Transaction (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016.

6. Section 271C penalty cannot be imposed for belated or non-payment of TDS: Supreme Court

[US Technologies International (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2023] 149 taxmann.com 144 (SC)]

The assessee, a private limited company, was engaged in a software development business. Nothing is to be added, or nothing is to be taken out of the penal provision.

It is noted that such amount would be disallowed permanently, i.e. it is not deductible in the year of payment [it was allowable prior to amendment basis some court rulings]. Accordingly, the employer needs to pay tax on such an amount, and he also needs to deposit such an amount to the relevant fund.

Moreover, principles or rules of interpretation have been devised to assist the Courts in the interpretation of statutes where the word or language used there are ambiguous and there is a doubt about the meaning thereof provided the doubt is real and not merely fanciful. So long as there is no ambiguity, conflict or absurdity in the statutory language, resort to any interpretative process to unfold the legislative intent becomes impermissible. The said view was taken by the apex Court in the following cases:

Keshavji Ravji v. CIT [183 ITR 1(SC)]

CAgIT v. Plantation Corpn. [247 ITR 155 (SC)]

CIT v. Anjum Ghaswala [252 ITR 1 (SC)]

Therefore, if any statutory provision is plain and unambiguous, admitting no second meaning, then no rule of interpretation needs to be employed and no extraneous considerations need to be imported. If the wording is clear and unambiguous, benefits which are not available under a section cannot be conferred by expanding or misinterpreting the words in that section. If there is no ambiguity in a provision, it cannot be read down.

Court in the case of Padmasundra Rao v. State of TN [255 ITR 147 (SC)] and Pandian Chemicals Limited v. CIT [262 ITR 278 (2003)] observed that the language employed in a statute is the determinative factor of legislative intent. The first and primary rule of construction is that the intention of the legislation must be found in the words used by the legislature itself.

In the case of Dalmia Biscuits v. CIT (194 ITR 749) it was observed that every word of a statute has to be assumed to have been deliberately and consciously incorporated therein by the legislature. Further, apex Court in the case of Mohammad v. CWT [224 ITR 672 (SC)] observed that if the language of a statute is clear and explicit, effect must be given to each word. One should look squarely at the words in the light of what is expressly stated and nothing can be implied so as to supply any assumed deficiency.

Conclusion

From the above detailed discussion, it can be seen that that the crucial aspect of intent behind introduction of section 36(1)(va) was not discussed by the Supreme Court in the Rajasthan State Beverages Corporation (Supra)case, while dismissing the Department SLP. Even the Rajasthan High Court decision did not discuss the crucial distinction between rationale behind deductibility of an employer's contribution under section 43B and an employee's contribution under section 36(1)(va) of the Act. In fact, the important controversy as highlighted above by various High Court rulings including in the recent case of Popular Vehicles (supra) has not been considered by the Supreme Court. Therefore, the controversy has not been conclusively resolved since by this interpretation, the whole purpose of enactment of section 36(1)(va) of the Act has not been considered. We have to see if the Supreme Court comes up with a detailed decision discussing the above aspect so as to finally resolve the controversy.

TDS and refunds

5. The TDS is not the actual revenue of the Government; it is only payment of tax in advance, which is adjusted against the actual tax liability of the assessee. In case of income-tax a good part of revenue is collected through TDS. The deductee has the right to claim credit of the TDS against his tax liability and this right gives rise to the refunds and problems related to refunds, which are increasing day-by-day.

The much-talked guidelines regarding IT ombudsman have the problems related to refunds as its top priority and the top four matters which are mentioned in the guidelines about which the assessee can file a complaint to the IT ombudsman are related to the issues concerned with refunds. This shows that the issue of refunds claim from the department is always a cause of harassment for the taxpayers.

The problems related to refunds as mentioned in the guidelines are detailed as under: —

(i)Delay in receiving refunds from the department.

(ii)Receiving envelops without refunds.

(iii)Non-adherence of first-in first-out method in issuing the refunds.

The service tax is still free from these side-effects but if TDS is applied to the service tax, then the service providers will have to wait for refunds from the department because of Cenvat credit, exemptions, etc., and have to face the same types of problems, like income-tax assessees.

Number of service receivers

6. The number of service receivers is very high compared to the service providers. As per the initial discussion, the TDS liability will only apply to certain class of the service receivers. It is further reported that the scheme of TDS is being introduced to avoid the leakage of revenue. Since the number of service receivers is much more than the number of service providers, there will be more tax depositing points as compared to the existing points. This will lead to a possibility of more leakage of revenue. Further, there is no evidence to prove the claim that the service receivers will deposit the tax more sincerely and honestly than the service providers. The scams and frauds related to the income-tax refunds are an indication of the fact that the system in this respect is not foolproof.

The administration of service tax is at present entrusted to the Central Excise and Customs Department and the taxpayer’s belief is that this is a stopgap arrangement and, hence, every year at the time of Budget there is a demand for a separate service tax department. Hence, at this level it will not be logical to give ‘Refund and TDS’ work to Central Excise and Custom Department, which is already burdened with excise matters.

Procedural hazards

7. The income-tax assessees are facing the procedural hazards of filing quarterly TDS returns and the whole burden of automation in this respect has been shifted on to the taxpayers who are spending their resources and valuable time to serve the Government by deducting, collecting and depositing the tax. But their grievances are too many and redressal of such grievances is very minimum and till date no steps have been taken to give them relief.

These all procedural hazards will have to be faced by the service receivers also if the TDS is introduced.

Section 201 provides the consequences in case of any failure to deduct or to pay the tax deducted at source. Sub-section (3) of Section 201 provides that no order deeming a deductor to be an assessee-in-default, on failure to deduct the tax from a person resident in India, shall be passed after the expiry of 7 years from the end of the financial year in which payment is made, or credit is given or after the expiry of 2 years from the end of the financial year in which correction statement is furnished, whichever is later. However, these time limits are applicable only when TDS defaults are related to payments made to a person resident in India. In other words, sub-section (3) does not apply if there is a default in the tax deduction with respect to payments made to a non-resident.

Pre-Budget discussion - TDS to service tax: Will it be viable?

Budget 2007 is round the corner and as per the recent indications the whole emphasis will be on service tax. A new concept is emerging in pre-Budget discussions, that is, to block the leakage of service tax, the system of TDS should be introduced in service tax also and according to this, the service receiver while making the payment to the service provider will deduct the service tax and deposit the same with the Government.

The author in this article throws light on the problems related to refunds and procedural hazards faced by service receivers and the question whether it will be viable and practically possible to introduce TDS system in service tax.

The concept of TDS

1. The concept of TDS can be understood from the Income-tax Law where it is widely applicable with respect to payment of salary, interest, commission, contract and sub-contract amount, etc. In this system tax at the prescribed rate is deducted from the payment made to the persons by the payer and deposited with the Government. The payee is getting the credit of the tax deducted by the certificate issued by the deducter. A new system of paper less TDS regime is also in offing and in coming years the TDS certificates vanish and the taxpayers will get the credit of the tax through electronic system automatically.

TDS on service tax

2. The service provider raises the service tax bill and if the TDS system is applied, then the service receiver at the time of payment of bill will deduct the service tax and deposit it with the Government. The service provider will get the credit of the service tax in his assessment on the strength of the certificate issued by the service receiver. The TDS certificate may be in paper format or in any other form in which it may be prescribed by the Government while introducing the scheme.

The present system

3. At present, barring a few exceptions, the service provider while issuing the bill, charges service tax in it and after receiving the payment of bill from the service receiver, the same is deposited with the Government after adjustment of the Cenvat credit available to the service provider.

Service tax is indirect tax

4. The service tax, like tax on sale of goods, is an indirect tax and the ultimate burden of the tax is to be borne by the service receiver. He may pass on the same to his consumer but in any case it is not the service provider who is bearing the burden of service tax. This fact has made the whole system of taxation totally different from the income-tax, which is the only tax where TDS provisions are applicable.

In case of other indirect tax, i.e., ‘VAT’ the TDS provisions are not generally applicable but in case of works contract these provisions are applicable because the works contracts are being taxed in a very special manner.

50. ITC matching mechanism of credit shown in Form GSTR-2B with credit shown in Form GSTR-3B.

The current manner of availing the credit and verification is as follows:

Section 16(2) of the CGST Act prescribes the condition for the availment of credit. The major conditions are that the recipient should have received the goods or services and that copies of invoices or other documents evidencing payment of tax are available with the recipient.

The supplier of goods or services is required to declare the supply in GSTR-1 every month or Form GSTR-1 through IFF quarterly. The information stated in this form, inter alia, includes the registration number of the recipient.

The portal prepares a statement of input tax credit for each registered person (recipient) in Form GSTR-2B, which should be availed as credit for that month as per the circular issued by the department.

In case of a difference in the amount of credit for any month shown in Form GSTR-3B with the amount in Form GSTR-2B, notice is issued to the recipient.

The recipient does not avail of the credit unless the invoice is accounted for in the books of accounts. This section presumes that the invoice of the supplier is accounted for in the books of account in the same month in which the supplier raises the invoice. Say the supplier has raised the invoice in the month of Nov-2025 for supplies made in November 2025. It is presumed by the above method that the invoice will be accounted for by the recipient in November 2025, and he will avail the credit in the same month.

As per Section 16(4) of the CGST Act, the recipient can avail of the GST credit by November following the end of the financial year. Thus, credit for the supply of Nov-2025 can be availed latest by 30th November 2026. Further, the annual return in Form GSTR-9 and Form GSTR-9C is required to be filed by December following the end of the financial year. Therefore, monitoring the availment of credit on a monthly basis when the law permits availment in subsequent months is leading to substantial problems and unnecessary issues of letters.

It is recommended that the department compare credit availment on a yearly basis rather than monthly, and that notices for differences in credit arising from a mismatch between GSTR-2B and the credit actually availed by the recipient be issued on a yearly basis instead of monthly. The formats of Form GSTR-9 and Form GSTR-9C shall be suitably amended to provide all the information required by the department, so that the audit verification is minimal.

IS THERE ANY LEGAL OBLIGATION TO DEDUCT TAX AT SOURCE ON PAYMENT OF SERVICE TAX AND OTHER ALLIED TAXES TO PAYEE ?

Introduction

1. With the levy of service tax and on bringing a large number of services under the ambit of service tax net, the question of deducting tax at source on payment of service tax has become significant. For example, an auditor raises a bill for audit fee for Rs. 1,12,360 (Comprising of Rs. 1 lakh for audit fee, Rs. 12,000 for service tax, Rs. 240 for education cess and Rs. 120 for secondary higher education cess). Now the question arises whether the client who pays fee to the auditor should deduct tax on Rs. 1,12,360 which is inclusive of Government taxes for Rs. 12,360 or on Rs. 1 lakh which is audit fee that goes to the pocket of the auditor and forms his income. There is a controversy on this issue. Some say that income-tax should be deducted at the rate of 10 per cent (applicable on payment to professionals) plus applicable surcharge, education cess and S.H.E.C. on income-tax and SC on the gross amount of Rs. 1,12,360 which is paid to the auditor under section 194J of the Income-tax Act, 1961 whereas others say that it should be deducted on Rs. 1 lakh which forms the income of the auditor.

Just to avoid litigation most of the clients deduct tax on the gross amount which is accepted by the recipients also since the recipient will get the full credit for the tax deducted at source and, therefore, he does not object to the excess tax deduction, if any, as the same is either adjusted against his tax liability or a refund is claimed by him in respect of excess tax deducted. On the other hand, the deductor client would not like to go into the litigation that may make him liable to pay any amount in future on account of charge of short deduction of TDS. It has been seen that in many cases notices for short deduction even for small amounts ranging from Rs. 100 to Rs. 200 are issued by the department pertaining to those years (exceeding 6 years) for which most of the assessees are not supposed to keep records. Section 149 of the Act states that no notice under section 148 shall be issued after expiry of 4 years from the end of relevant assessment year and in certain cases (where income chargeable to tax which has escaped assessment amounts to 1 lakh or more), the period is six years.

In view of the above provision, generally assessees do not preserve accounting records for over 6 years. Under the Act, there is no limitation to recover the shortfall of tax deduction and, therefore, in cases where petty demands are raised for over six years, normally the assessee deposits the same to avoid litigation or to avoid botheration to satisfy the assessing authorities as to the fact that the same are not payable.

To avoid litigation normally assessees by and large deduct tax on gross amount payable to the service provider including the amount of service tax and allied taxes which is accepted by the persons whose tax is deducted for the simple reason that he will get the full benefit of tax deducted at source and, therefore, he does not object.

However, in the following paragraphs an effort has been made to know the legal status of the query whether to deduct the tax at source on payment of income or on the gross amount payable, which is inclusive of service tax and other applicable taxes.

Relevant provisions

2. Income-tax at source is deductible under the provisions of sections 192 to 195 of the Act on various payments which form the income of the recipients. Each section to know on what amount tax is deductible at source is discussed in paras to follow :

Thus, tax is deductible on the amount of income which is subject to tax and not on the gross income which is payable to the recipient employee.

35. Notional interest on security deposit received by landlord for letting out the property Deposit of security amount is a usual practice at the time of letting out a property. There is no provision in the Income-tax Act to calculate and include the notional interest on such security amount while calculating the income from house property.

The Courts have consistently held that notional interest on interest free security deposit shall not be taken into consideration while computing ALV of house property let out by the taxpayers.

It is suggested that the upcoming Budget should bring suitable amendments to end the litigations on this count. If the security deposit is reasonable (equivalent to average rent for 3 months) no notional interest should be added to the income from house property.

36. Deductibility of discount given on ESOPs

Some of recent judicial pronouncements suggest that the tax fraternity is grappling with the controversy on the tax treatment of the discounts on the shares issued to the employees under ESOPs.

The revenue has been contending that the said discounts can never be allowed as deductions on the following grounds:

(a)

The discount offered under ESOP is not in the nature of expenditure;

(b)

Such discount is not given in the normal course of business carried on by the Company;

(c)

Such discount merely represents short receipt of premium on issue of shares. If the receipt of premium is not taxable, the short receipt of such premium should also not be allowed as deduction;

(d)

At the most, such discount could be considered as a short capital receipt or a sort of capital expenditure.

Conversely, the Companies issuing ESOP's argue that the primary object of an ESOP is not to raise share capital but to earn profit by securing the consistent and concentrated efforts of its dedicated employees during the vesting period. Therefore, such discount should be construed as nothing but a part of remuneration. Such discounted premium on shares is a substitute for giving direct incentive in cash for availing of the services of the employees.

In order to avoid unnecessary litigations, it would be prudent for the Finance Minister to clarify this stand on the tax treatment of discounts on issue of shares under ESOP. The industry expects a clarification stating that the discounts on ESOP scheme should be amortized over the vesting period.

37. Inclusion of carbon credits under section 2(24)

A new section 115BBG was inserted under Income-tax Act with effect from assessment year 2018-19 to provide that where the total income of the assessee includes any income from transfer of carbon credit, such income shall be taxable at the rate of 10% on gross basis. The amendment was made to avoid controversy whether the income from sale of carbon credit shall be treated as capital receipt or not?

Though the Finance Act has made much needed amendment through introduction of section 115BBG. Yet, no amendment has been made to section 28 to hold that any profit on transfer of carbon credit would be treated as business income. Further, no amendment has been made to the definition of 'income' in section 2(24) to provide that any such sum received upon transfer of carbon credits is income. In the absence of such provisions in the Act and due to various judgments holding that income on transfer of carbon credits is capital receipt, it is a moot point as to whether the amounts received upon such transfer are taxable as income under section 2(24) notwithstanding the insertion of section 115BBG.

So, it is expected that amendment shall be made to section 28 and 2(24) to bring the regularity in the provisions.

38. Rate of depreciation for intangible assets in case of power generating units

The Income-tax (Amendment) Act, 1998 has provided an option to the undertakings engaged in generation or generation and distribution of power to claim depreciation by using straight line method. However, the Appendix IA to Income-tax Rules, 1962 doesn't provide for any rate of depreciation on the Intangible assets on straight line basis. Thus, power generating units can opt for such depreciation method only in respect of tangible assets. It is recommended that the rate of depreciation for intangible assets in case of power generating units should also be introduced in Appendix IA.

39. Depreciation on Goodwill

The Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Smifs Securities Ltd. [2012] 24 taxmann.com 222 (SC) held that the goodwill arising on amalgamation of companies would be eligible for depreciation as it is covered under Explanation 3(b) to Section 32(1) under the expression 'any other business or commercial rights of a similar nature'. After the judgment of the Apex Court, various High Courts have taken the similar stand.

It is recommended that the definition of intangible asset [as provided in the Explanation 3(b) to Section 32(1)] should include purchased goodwill, i.e., goodwill arising on amalgamation of companies, for the purpose of depreciation on intangible assets.

3.3 Issue-3: Role of DRP- The order of re-assessment proposed by the AO, viz., enhancing the income equivalent to the amounts disclosed in TDS certificates was approved by DRP even without considering the method of accounting followed by the taxpayer.

The assessee also contended that if the entire royalty amounts disclosed in the TDS certificates were adopted as income, the corresponding TDS amounts ought to have been given credit, in which case levy of interest under section 234B would not have arisen.

The Tribunal held that the draft order of the Assessing Officer was not examined in the right perspective by the DRP. It held that the DRP had failed in its duty in resolving the dispute/objections of the assessee and had approved of the order of Assessing Officer without application of his mind.

Since the order of the Assessing Officer was after the approval of the DRP, the order of the Assessing Officer became an appealable order directly to the Tribunal as per section 254(1)(e).

3.4 Issue-4: Credit for TDS- Section 199 of the Income-tax Act, read with rule 37BA presently governs the credit for tax deduction at source. In this case, the assessee had not claimed credit for TDS for the entire amount of tax deducted at source by the payer for the reason that the entire sum was not offered as income chargeable to tax. Again, the issue hinged on and revolved around the method of accounting consistently followed by the taxpayer.

As the taxpayer had followed cash system of accounting, notwithstanding fact that the tax was deducted at source by the payer as per the mercantile system of accounting followed by him, the entire amount of TDS could not be claimed as credit, since the matching income was not admitted for tax assessment.

It may be noted that in IRB Infrastructure Ltd. v. ITO [2008] 115 ITD 374 (Mum.) when a particular method of accounting or accounting policy has been accepted by the revenue, it is not permissible to depart from the same, unless there is some compelling evidence justifying the departure.

When the assessee has followed cash system of accounting for more than a decade and such system has been accepted in the preceding years, it cannot be rejected or ignored for tax assessment in a subsequent year. Thus, the principle of consistency aided the taxpayer in Johnson & Johnson's case(supra).

Conclusion

4. The facts of the case of Johnson & Johnson (supra) and the legal precedents discussed above lead us to the following conclusions:

The method of accounting would decide the quantum of income chargeable to tax. However, in the case of non-residents if there is no DTAA or the DTAA does not mandate taxation of income on receipt/cash basis, then the Supreme Court's decision in Standard Triumph Motor Co. Ltd. (supra)will apply. To put it differently, in the case of non-residents the income credited to their account by the resident-payee is chargeable to tax the moment the income is credited ignoring the method of accounting followed by the recipient-non-resident. However, if the DTAA mandates taxation of income on receipt basis then the DTAA would overrule the Supreme Court's dictum.

When the income is offered to tax in consonance with the method of accounting consistently followed by the taxpayer, credit for tax deducted at source must be given only to that part of income for which tax has been deducted at source. Credit for TDS cannot be claimed nor can be granted, where the corresponding income is not chargeable or offered to tax.

When the assessee has made a true and full disclosure of the fact of total income vis-a-vis the income chargeable to tax as per the method of accounting consistently followed, backed up by the DTAA, there is no scope for interpreting the same as escapement of income subsequently, unless some other fresh material or basis comes to light. If there is no fresh material than what is subsisting on record, the re-assessment would be taken as change of opinion, which is not valid in law. The Supreme Court's decision in the case of Kelvinator of India Ltd. (supra) would prevail.

Q45. What are the modes for filing a return of income?

The filing of income tax returns must be electronic, either online or using the offline utility provided by the Income Tax Department. However, individuals aged 80 or above who are submitting returns in ITR-1 or ITR-4 have the option to file in paper mode.

If the return of income is filed through electronic mode, then the assessee has the following options:

(a)

E-filing using a Digital Signature (DSC)

(b)

E-filing without a Digital Signature or

(c)

E-filing through Aadhaar OTP

(d)

E-filing under Electronic Verification Code (EVC).

If the return of income is filed using a DSC, Aadhaar OTP or under EVC, then there is no requirement to send the signed copy, ITR-V (i.e., acknowledgement of return filed electronically) to Bengaluru CPC. However, where the return is filed without DSC, Aadhaar OTP or EVC, the assessee shall send the signed copy of ITR V to the following address either by ordinary post or by speed post only:

"Income Tax Department – Centralized Processing Centre, Income-tax Department, Bengaluru -560500."

Q46. What is the time limit for sending a signed copy of ITR-V to CPC or verifying the return furnished online?

The time limit for e-verification or submission of ITR-V is 30 days from the date of filing of the return of income electronically2. If the return of income is not verified within 30 days from the date of uploading or by the due date for filing the return as specified in the IT Act, whichever is later, the return will be considered invalid due to non-verification3. It should be noted that if the return is filed before the due date but the return is verified after the expiry of 30 days, which falls after the due date for filing the return of income, the return shall be considered to be a belated return of income.

For instance, you upload your income tax return on July 1st, 2025. You're required to verify it within 30 days, which means by July 31st, 2025. However, you can verify it until December 31st, 2025, which is the due date for filing a belated return. If you verify it after 15th September# but before December 31st, your return will be treated as a belated return.

# The due date for furnishing the return of income for the Assessment year 2025-26 has been extended from July 31, 2025, to September 15, 2025, vide Circular no. 06/2025, dated 27-05-2025.

Q47. What happens if I do not verify my ITR by December 31, 2025?

If you do not verify or submit the ITR-V by December 31, 2025, which is the final verification date for the Assessment Year 2025-26, the return will be treated as invalid due to non-verification.

PL SUBRAMANIAN*

AVAILMENT OF CENVAT CREDIT

In this article, the author has outlined the situations where service tax paid cannot be denied on the ground that service tax is not applicable in the light of relevant case-laws. The other issues discussed here include : applicability of the time-limit for taking CENVAT credit and utilization of CENVAT credit in case of payment of advance capital goods and centralised registration.

Service Tax Paid - Cannot be denied on the ground that service tax is not applicable : relevant case-laws

1. (i) In Maersk India (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [Order No. A/475 (Mum.) of 2008, dated 16-5-2008] - The appellant was registered under the category of ‘Storage & warehousing service’ and ‘Maintenance and repair services’. It got a part of its empty containers repaired through its sub-contractors. The sub-contractors charged service tax on the ‘repair charges’ charged to the appellant and, in turn, the appellant had taken credit of the service tax paid.

CENVAT credit was denied on the ground that sub-contractors did not have service tax liability. It was held by the Tribunal that once service tax has been paid by the service provider, the same cannot be questioned at the receiver’s end and, accordingly, credit cannot be denied.

(ii) Vodafone Essar Digilink Ltd. v. CCE [S.O. No. 15 (Delhi) of 2008 dated 2-1-2008] - BSNL provided service to the appellant and paid service tax on port and space charges. The appellant had taken credit of the service tax paid and credit was denied on the ground that BSNL was not liable to pay service tax in respect of port and space charges.

It was held by the Tribunal that since the payment of service tax by BSNL was not challenged, credit cannot be denied. In this case, pre-deposit of tax and penalty was waived.

(iii) CCE v. Purity Flexpack Ltd. [T.A. No. 92 (Guj.) of 2006 dated 23-11-2006] - The manufacturer had paid Excise duty at the rate of 24 per cent instead of the correct rate of 16 per cent and the buyer of the goods had taken credit of the full amount. It was held that the assessee was entitled to take full credit, as the department had not initiated any action at the supplier’s, i.e., manufacturers’, end.

Supply of components and parts and erection of plant

2. In Rajarambapu Patil SSK Ltd. v. CCE [2008] 11 STR 437 (Trib. - Mum.), the appellant entered into two contracts with a contractor - one for supply of components and parts and another for erection at the appellant’s site. He had taken credit of the duty paid on the components and parts which were used in setting up of the plant and the department held that he was not entitled to credit and the components and parts were inputs of the contractor who supplied and assembled them at the appellant’s site since it was he who used it to manufacture the plant.

The Tribunal held that the contention of the department was incorrect and the appellant was eligible to avail the credit of the duty paid on the parts and components.

Bill without name of service receiver

3. In CCE v. Diamond Cements [2009] 18 STT 151 (New Delhi - CESTAT), the Tribunal held that a certificate from the service provider that the service had been rendered to the appellant can be accepted as a valid document for availing CENVAT credit where the bills did not mention the name and address of the appellant. However, it will be advisable to ask the service provider to enter the name and address of the service receiver in the bills instead of taking separate letter.

Time-Limit

4. Rule 4 of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 provides for rules for taking CENVAT credit. The relevant rules are reproduced below for ready reference.

Input : Rule 4(1) - CENVAT credit in respect of inputs may be taken immediately on receipt of the inputs in the factory of the manufacturer or in the premises of the provider of output service.

Input Service : Rule 4(7) - CENVAT credit in respect of input service shall be allowed, on or after the day on which payment is made of the value of input service and the service tax is paid or payable as is indicated in invoice, bill or, as the case may be, challan referred to in rule 9.

provider should issue Invoice when part of service tax is payable by service provider?

Where the service provider is liable to pay part of service tax (25% in case of manpower supply and 50% in case of works contract), he should charge only that part in his invoice and indicate that balance is payable by the service receiver - view confirmed in para 10.1.2 of CBE&C's Taxation of Services : 'An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012. It may be noted that even if service provider does not charge service tax in his invoice, the service receiver is still liable to pay his part of service tax (25% or 50% as applicable), since the small service provider's exemption is not available to him - Para 10.1.3 of CBE&C's Taxation of Services : 'An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012.

Service provider is charging service tax on 25%/50% and balance is paid by the service receiver. While deducting tax under income-tax provisions, whether TDS should be on his invoice amount or after including service tax payable by the service receiver?

Section 194C(1) of the Income-tax Act states that any person responsible for paying any sum to any contractor for carrying out any work (including supply of labour for carrying out any work) shall, at the time of credit of such sum to the account of contractor or at the time of payment, whichever is earlier, deduct an amount equal to specified percentage of 'such sum' as income-tax.

'Such sum' means sum credited to account of contractor or paid to him. The 'service tax' amount payable by service receiver is never credited to the account of the contractor. Hence, in my view, the quantum of service tax payable by the service receiver is not required to be considered while deducting TDS.

Can the service receiver avail of Cenvat credit of tax paid by him under reverse charge?

The assessee paying service tax under reverse charge method will be eligible to avail of Cenvat credit of the service tax paid on the basis of GAR-7 Challan (earlier TR-6 Challan) by which the tax is paid [Rule 9(1)(e) of the Cenvat Credit Rules, as amended w.e.f. 1-5-2006]. The assessee should pay service tax in cash, i.e., without utilising the Cenvat credit.

He can avail of Cenvat credit on basis of the challan, if otherwise eligible for Cenvat credit - Para of CBE&C's Taxation of Services : 'An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012.

Note that in case of some services (e.g., motor vehicle hire for transport of passengers, construction of factory or office building, GTA service after place of removal), Cenvat credit is not available in view of restrictions put on definition of 'input service.' In such cases, Cenvat credit will not be available just because service tax is paid under reverse charge. Even in such cases, service tax is payable in cash and it is cost to the assessee.

Can the service provider avail of Cenvat credit when he is liable to pay 25% or 50% service tax?

Even if service provider is liable to pay service tax on 25% or 50% amount, he is entitled to entire 100% Cenvat credit available to him. (This was indeed clarified in Para C.2 sub-para 15 of Circular No. 334/1/2012-TRU, dated 16-3-2012.

Can a service receiver ask the service provider to pay entire amount of service tax instead of service receiver paying the same?

When a statutory liability is fixed, it cannot be shifted to another person by an agreement. Please do not use such short cuts.

In Vantage Security v. CCE [2007] 7 STT 300 (New Delhi - CESTAT), service tax was paid by service receiver, though it was payable by service provider. It was held that the payment was invalid and demand of service tax from service provider was valid. Assessee was asked to deposit part of the amount for granting stay.

Legally payment of service tax by service provider is not correct when service receiver is liable. This should not be done.

In the initial stages, Tribunal may take a lenient view and ignore a technical lapse. However, this should not be followed as a routine practice.

Can Service Provider claim refund of excess Cenvat credit?

In case of reverse charge, the service provider is either not liable to pay service tax or is liable to pay service tax at reduced rates. In such case, the service provider can claim refund of excess Cenvat credit with him, which he is unable to utilise as per procedure as may be prescribed by CBE&C - Rule 5B of the Cenvat Credit Rules as inserted w.e.f. 1-7-2012.

So far, no procedure has been prescribed. However, in my view it is advisable to file a refund claim within one year to keep the claim alive.

(a)

Removal of the requirement to file in quadruplicate

The requirement to submit the application in quadruplicate is outdated, as Rule 44E was amended to remove this requirement, effective May 5, 2022, due to the transition to digital/email-based filing. 25. TDS on Salary and Provident Fund

As per ITA 1961

Section 192 governs TDS on salary. It mandates tax deduction at the average rate on the estimated income under the head "Salaries" at the time of payment.

Sub-section (6) of Section 192 specifically deals with the valuation of salary paid in foreign currency, stating that such salary must be converted into Indian Rupees at the prescribed exchange rates for the purpose of TDS.

Further, Section 192A mandates 10% TDS on taxable payments from recognised provident funds, where the accumulated balance is included in total income and is Rs. 50,000 or more. This section contains a non-obstante clause, meaning it overrides other provisions of the Act.

As per ITB 2025

Clause 392 of the Bill consolidates the provisions of Sections 192 and 192A.

(a)

Sub-clauses (1) to (6) of Clause 392 provide for TDS on salary at the average rate, based on estimated income for the tax year. However, there is no provision corresponding to the current Section 192(6) regarding salary paid in foreign currency.

(b)

Clause 392(7) provides for 10% TDS on the accumulated balance withdrawn from a recognised provident fund, where such amount is taxable and is Rs. 50,000 or more. Unlike Section 192A, this clause does not contain a non-obstante clause.

Select Committee Recommendation

(a)

Clarity on TDS rate for recognised provident fund

The Committee observed that Clause 392(7)(a) lacked clarity on whether TDS should apply at the average rate (as used for salary under Clause 392(1)) or at the flat rate of 10% (as stated in Clause 392(7)).To avoid misinterpretation and ensure consistency with current law, the Committee recommended inserting a non-obstante clause to clarify that 10% TDS shall apply in such cases. The Ministry accepted this recommendation.

(b)

Inclusion of a provision for salary paid in foreign currency

The Committee noted that the Bill inadvertently omitted provisions corresponding to Section 192(6), which governs the conversion of foreign currency salary into INR at prescribed rates for TDS purposes.

The absence of such a provision could lead to inconsistent valuation, confusion, and potential litigation. The Committee recommended that a suitable provision be inserted in Clause 392 to prescribe conversion at the notified forex rates. The Ministry also accepted this recommendation.

26. Certificate for lower or nil deduction /collection of tax

Clause 395 of the ITB consolidates and simplifies several provisions of the ITA, such as Sections 195(2), 197, 197A, 203, 206C(9), and 206C(10), which relate to certificates for lower or nil deduction/collection of tax.

The Committee noted that Clause 395(1) removes the term "Nil deduction" which is explicitly present in Section 197 of the existing Act. The Department stated that "lower deduction" is meant to include "nil deduction" as well, and that clarification will be issued via administrative instructions. However, the Committee felt that replacing "nil" with "lower" may lead to ambiguity, especially in practical cases such as foreign banks seeking exemption from TDS on customer payments or loss-making entities or non-residents availing of treaty benefits.

To avoid confusion and ensure clarity in law, the Committee recommended that the word "nil" be reinstated in Clause 395(1), rather than relying on future administrative guidance.

27. Powers regarding discovery and production of evidence

As per ITA 1961

Section 131(1A) empowers specified senior officers (like Principal Director General, Director General, etc.) to exercise the powers of discovery and investigation even if no proceedings are pending, but only in relation to a person or class of persons within their jurisdiction. This ensures that powers are territorially restricted to prevent overreach.

As per ITB 2025

Clause 246(2)(b) allows similar powers to certain officers for inquiry or investigation without any reference to jurisdiction. The omission of the jurisdictional requirement raises the possibility that officers may act beyond their territorial authority.

Section 194-O casts an obligation on e-commerce operators to deduct tax at 1% (5% if PAN/Aadhar is not furnished) while making payment/credit to e-commerce participants for sale of goods/services facilitated through its platform.

(a)

Exclude transactions where no payment is routed through an e-commerce operator

Section 194-O also mandates that the e-commerce operator must deduct and pay tax on behalf of the e-commerce participant, even in the case that the ecommerce participant is receiving full payment directly from the customer. In this scenario, the e-commerce operator may face difficulties in recovering TDS from the e-commerce participant. Consequently, the cost of such TDS will have to be borne by the e-commerce operator, if not reimbursed by the participant.

In view of the above, appropriate clarifications may be provided that in case a transaction materializes directly between a customer and an e-commerce participant, with payment being made directly to the e-commerce participant and with no payment is ever due from the e-commerce operator to the ecommerce participant, it will not be covered within the scope of section 194-O.

(b)

Exclude e-commerce operators providing only listing services

There are certain platforms which only provide listing and information of the products on their website and do not participate at all in the sale process. In such cases, the role of the platform is merely limited to advertising the product.

However, given the wide meaning of the word 'facilitated', these e-commerce operators may fall withing the ambit of section 194-O. In view of such practical challenges, it is recommended that said category of e-commerce operators (those whomerely provide listing of price, referrals and product information) should be excluded from the scope of section 194-O.

Clarification for transactions carried out through email/telephones

Given that the term "digital or electronic platform or facility" can be subject to wide interpretations, it can even cover cases where sale or services are carried out through the medium of "e-mail" or "telephone". The assessee claimed refund of service tax on the ground that it was not liable to pay service tax on sponsorship service. The assessee also claimed Cenvat credit on service tax in respect of business exhibition service. The lower authorities disallowed the claim regarding sponsorship service, on the ground that service tax was charged from the service receiver and had rightly been deposited with the Government. The Cenvat credit on business exhibition service was denied on the ground that the payment in respect of bills was made in the months of June, 2006 to October, 2006, whereas Cenvat credit was taken after six months in March, 2007, which itself was not admissible.

As regards the refund claim of the sponsorship service, admittedly the service tax amount was not separately shown in the invoices for domestic clients. The assessee claimed that in some cases service tax was refunded to the clients. The very fact that in some cases service tax was refunded to the customers showed that in all the cases the amount collected included the element of service tax. In such a situation as rightly observed by the lower authorities, how the chartered accountant of the assessee came to the conclusion that in respect of domestic clients, the amount charged did not include service tax, was not explained and did not appear to be logical. Under the circumstances of the instant case, the certificate of chartered accountant was not based on facts and from the documents, the only conclusion emerged that in respect of domestic clients, the assessee had collected the service tax. Therefore, the claim for refund had been rejected correctly.

On the issue of Cenvat credit on business exhibition service the assessee raised two points to the effect that the amount paid initially was not the final one and the finalization took some time and, therefore, credit was taken much later, and that in terms of sub-rule (7) of rule 4, there was no time-limit prescribed. Unlike Cenvat credit on inputs/capital goods, where credit can be taken immediately on receipt of inputs/capital goods, in the case of service tax the credit can be taken only after the payment is made in respect of the bills raised for providing service and the rule also requires that service tax is also paid. Therefore, the service receiver is obliged not only to make payment but would also be responsible to ensure that service tax has been paid. In the instant case, admittedly, the payments were made from June, 2006 to October, 2006 but it did not come out clearly as to whether there were different services and in respect of how many service tax was paid in June, etc. In view of the obligations cast on the service receiver, the time taken by the assessee to take the credit did not appear unreasonable especially in view of the fact that exact delay in respect of each credit had not been brought out in the records. Further, the assessee also claimed that the amount paid was not final and only after the service was fully received, the actual amount payable was determined. Under these circumstances, the benefit of doubt was to be extended to the assessee and it had to be held that credit had been taken within a reasonable time and the assessee was eligible to same.

Currently, salaried employees are allowed a standard deduction of INR 50,000. The question which was referred in the instant case was whether the provisions of rule 6(3)(b) will come into force, despite the fact that the assessee had reversed the Cenvat credit attributable on the inputs used in the manufacture of exempted final products. The assessee submitted that rule 6(3)(b) would not be violated if the credit taken on the common inputs used in the manufacture of exempted product, is reversed by the manufacturer. The revenue submitted that once an assessee opts to avail the Cenvat credit of the duty paid on common inputs, which are used for dutiable and exempted goods, he does not have an option to reverse the credit availed on the quantity of common inputs used in the manufacture of exempted goods and is perforce required to reverse 8 per cent or 10 per cent of the value of the exempted goods cleared, subject to the deductions allowed.

The Tribunal held that a plain reading of rule 6 clearly obligates the manufacturer of dutiable and exempted goods to follow the procedure while availing Cenvat credit on the inputs. Rule 6(1) specifically prohibits Cenvat credit being allowed on such quantity of inputs as used in the manufacture of exempted goods. The provisions of rule 6(2) would indicate that the manufacturer, who avails Cenvat credit in respect of common inputs, is required to maintain separate accounts for receipt, consumption and inventory of inputs meant for use in the manufacture of final products. The provisions of rule 6(3)(a) and (b) further indicate how the manufacturer has to follow the procedure if he is not maintaining separate account. On a plain reading of rule 6(3)(b) it would transpire that the manufacturer who has availed Cenvat credit on common inputs does not have any other option but to pay 8 per cent or 10 per cent of total price (excluding sales tax and other taxes, if any, paid on such goods), of the exempted final products charged by the manufacturer for the sale of such goods at the time of their clearance from the factory. Thus, reversal of the credit taken or availed under rule 6 is not contemplated by the rules. It was found that these provisions are in pari materia with the provisions of rule 57CC and rule 57AD of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. Combined reading of rule 57CC (1) and 57CC (9) would indicate that rule 6(3)(b) has been carved out of a combination of the said sub-rule of rule 57CC.

Thus, it would be appropriate to explicitly provide that the entire compensation amount and any accompanying interest paid to claimants shall be exempt from tax.

Relaxation from 1st proviso to Section 68 in case of loans taken from banks Section 68 of the Income-tax Act provides that if any sum is found credited in the books of accounts and the assessee offers no explanation about the nature and source thereof or the Explanation offered by him is not satisfactory, in the opinion of the Assessing Officer, the sum so credited may be charged to income tax as the income of the assessee of that previous year.

The Finance Act, 2022 inserted a new proviso to provide that the nature and source of the loan, borrowing or any other liability credited in the books of an assessee shall be treated as explained only if:

(a)

the person in whose name such credit is recorded also offers an explanation about the nature and source of such sum so credited; and

(b)

In the opinion of the Assessing Officer, such an explanation has been found to be satisfactory.

This newly inserted proviso emphasises the sum credited by way of loans, borrowings or any other liability of an assessee, irrespective of the status of the lender.

Thus, it has created a genuine hardship for those who have obtained loans from Banks, NBFCs, and Public Financial Institutions. There should be no question about the genuineness and creditworthiness of loans taken from these institutions. Therefore, it is recommended that Govt. amends Section 68 to carve out an exception for the loans taken from these institutions.

Expectations and Recommendations for 'Penalties'

43. Reference of Section 271AA and 271G is required in Section 253

Section 271AA lays down the penalty for failure to keep information in respect of an International Transaction. Under this provision, AO or CIT(A) may impose a penalty of a sum equal to 2% of the value of each international transaction or specified domestic transaction entered into by the taxpayer.

Similarly, Section 271G imposes a penalty for failure to furnish Information or documents relating to International Transactions. Under this section, the AO or TP Officer or CIT(A) may impose a penalty of a sum equal to 2% of the value of the international transaction or specified domestic transaction for each such failure.

Section 253 enlists the orders against which appeals to the Appellate Tribunal can be filed. It should be noted that the reference to Section 271AA and Section 271G still needs to be included in Section 253. Both these provisions give the CIT(A) powers to levy a penalty for failure to keep and furnish information relating to the international transaction.

Thus, it is recommended that a reference be provided for orders passed under Sections 271AA and 271G under Section 253.

44. Start-ups may be penalised for not fulfilling conditions under Section 80-IAC

Section 80-IAC does not contain any provision to withdraw the deduction if the start-up fails to fulfil the prescribed conditions. It is apprehended that an amendment could be made to Section 80-IAC to withdraw the deduction if the assessee company fails to comply with the conditions prescribed in the DPIIT's notification.

(Read more : Deduction to an eligible start-up on Taxmann.com/Practice)

Expectations and Recommendations for 'Prosectuions'

45. Proviso to Section 276B granting relief from TDS-related prosecution should have retrospective effect

Section 276B provides that failure to deposit TDS as required under Chapter XVII-B or to pay/ensure payment of tax as mandated under Section 115-O(2), the proviso to Section 194B, the first proviso to Section 194R(1), the proviso to Section 194S(1), or Section 194BA(2) is punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term ranging from 3 months to 7 years, along with a fine.

Further, Section 276BB provides for the launch of prosecution if a person fails to pay the tax collected by him. Such an offence is punishable with rigorous imprisonment of 3 months to 7 years and with a fine.

The Finance (No. 2) Act 2024 has inserted a proviso to Section 276B to provide immunity from prosecution for failure to deposit TDS if payment has been made to the government's credit at any time before filing the TDS return. This proviso has been inserted with prospective effect. Consequently, no immunity is provided in the pending case.

It is recommended that this proviso should be given a retrospective operation to provide immunity in the old cases. Further, it is recommended to introduce a similar provision in Section 276BB to offer relief in prosecutions related to TCS.

Consequence of failure to deduct or pay [Section 201]

8.5 Under section 201, a person is deemed to be an assessee-in-default if there is a failure to deduct tax at source or for failure to deposit the tax deducted at source after such tax has been deducted. The persons covered under the ambit of section 201 are:

(i) person referred to in section 200;

(ii) the principal officer and the company of which he is the principal officer in the cases referred to in section 194 [relating to deduction of tax at source on dividends].

Section 200(1) provides that any person deducting any tax at source in accordance with the provisions of Chapter XVII shall pay the sum so deducted to the Central Government or as the Board directs within the prescribed time. Since section 200 applies to persons deducting tax, and since it has been used in section 201, a view has been expressed that the provisions of section 201(1) do not cover failure to deduct tax at source. In order to counter this view, section 201(1) has been substituted with effect from 1-6-2002 to clarify that where a person, including the principal officer of a company,

(i) who is required to deduct any sum in accordance with the provisions of the Act; or

(ii) referred to in section 192(1A), being an employer,

does not deduct, or after so deducting fails to pay, or does not pay, the whole or any part of the tax, as required by or under the Act, he shall be deemed to an assessee in default under section 201.

A similar amendment has also been carried out in Explanation to section 191 with retrospective effect from 1-6-2003.

Dematerialisation of TDS and TCS certificates [Sections 203 & 206C]

8.6 An assessee is entitled to credit in respect of tax deducted at source (‘TDS’) and tax collected at source (‘TCS’) on the basis of a certificate issued by the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source. Such certificate has to be enclosed with the return of income to claim the credit.

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2004 proposed dematerialisation of TDS and TCS certificates and, inter alia1, provided that on and after 1-4-2005:

◆ the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source should file quarterly statements with the income-tax authority or authorised person;

◆ such authority or person would furnish a statement of tax deducted or collected at source (‘the Statement’) to the payee or buyer;

◆ the person responsible for deducting or collecting tax at source need not furnish certificate to the payee or buyer; and

◆ the payee or buyer would be entitled to the credit for TDS or TCS based on the statement furnished by such authority or person.

8.4-5 Credit for the tax deducted or collected - The provision in relation to :—

TDS [section 199(3)], reads as follows: "where any deduction is made. . . on or after the 1st day of April, 2005 and paid to the Central Government, the amount of tax deducted and specified in the statement referred to in section 203AA shall be treated as tax paid on behalf of the person referred to in sub-section (1)... and credit shall be given to him for the amount so deducted in the assessment... without production of certificate." (Emphasis supplied)

TCS [first proviso to section 206C(4)] reads: "provided that where any amount is collected... on or after 1st day of April, 2005 and paid... to the credit of the Central Government, the amount of tax collected and specified in statement referred to... shall be deemed as payment of tax on behalf of the person from whom the amount has been collected and credit shall be given to him for the amount so collected in the assessment... without production of certificate." (Emphasis supplied)

Thus, the amount of tax deducted/collected and specified in the Statement would be treated as tax paid on behalf of the payee/buyer. It appears, the payee/buyer would get credit for such tax deducted/collected on his/her behalf. For whatever reasons, the amount of tax deducted/collected is not specified in the Statement, the amount not specified would not be treated as tax deducted/collected on behalf of the payee/buyer and credit will not be available for the same to the payee/buyer.

In this connection an issue may arise about the treatment of tax deducted or collected and specified in the statement but not paid by the payer/collector. If appears that to the extent tax deducted/collected, whether specified in the statement or not the recovery cannot be enforced against the payee/buyer, for the following reasons :

(i)

Section 203AA and second proviso to section 206C(5), respectively provide that the prescribed income-tax authorities or authorised person shall prepare and collect the statement of tax deducted/paid [under section 192(1A)] on tax collected.

| How to deposit the TDS? | (a) A corporate assessee and other assessees (who are subject to tax audit under section 44AB) will have to make payment of tax (including TDS) electronically through internet banking facility or by way of debit cards.1 To deposit the tax, the deductor has to fill the Challan No. ITNS 281 or Form 26QB or Form 26QC or Form 26QD or Form 26QE. (b) Other deductors can deposit the tax so deducted into any branch of the Reserve Bank of India or the State Bank of India or of any authorized bank. It is not necessary for the assessee to make payment of taxes from his own account in an authorized bank. An assessee can make electronic payment of taxes also from the account of any other person. However, the challan for making such payment must clearly indicate the Tax Deduction and Collection Account Number (TAN) of the assessee on whose behalf the payment is made. |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| Consequences of Failure to Deposit TDS | If any person responsible for deduction of tax at source fails to deduct or after deduction fails to pay the same to the credit of the Central Government, then he shall be deemed to be an assessee in default and liable to pay interest or penalty. If a deductor after deducting the tax, fails to deposit the same to the credit of Central Government then he may also be prosecuted under section 276B. |  |  |  |  |  |  |
